The traditional reinforcement learning method is inefficient due to its focus on a specific reward function, which can result in limited policy performance when applied to varying environments. In contrast, our approach integrates an evolutionary algorithm with a reinforcement learning technique to create a more versatile policy. The flow of our evolution-based reinforcement learning method involves initially creating diverse policy trajectories using an evolutionary operator, followed by rewarding the most effective movements with a reinforcement learning mechanism. By repeating this process, a quadruped robot can develop a range of versatile gaits. The performance of our evolution-based reinforcement learning method is demonstrated through practical tests on a physically interactive quadruped robot, where it quickly learns a variety of adaptive gaits to navigate different scenarios. Our understanding of the complex interactions between the atmosphere and aerosols
requires frequent and precise measurements of aerosol properties. To address this
need, we've developed two novel methods - AEROSTAR and AEROFIL - which leverage
photometry techniques to estimate aerosol optical properties by analyzing the bright
stars. AEROFIL calculates the phase function and other key properties by capturing
images of the stars under different orientations. In contrast, AEROSTAR determines
the optical depth by measuring the star's brightness along the line of sight and uses
external data sources to calculate the phase function and other properties. Both
methods are now available in the Aerosol package for Python. Notably, our approach
has been shown to provide accurate measurements, with a particular strength being
the ability to estimate optical depth and other properties during twilight and
dusk/dawn hours. This capability is particularly valuable for ground-based solar energy
monitoring. By combining AEROFIL and AEROSTAR, we can significantly shorten the
time needed to collect reliable aerosol data, from hours to just 10 minutes. This
merged technique is also robust in the presence of inhomogeneous aerosols and has
been successfully tested using data from the Big Bear Observatory and the Izaña
Observatory. This research marks an important milestone in the ongoing development
of solar photometry, ultimately paving the way for a solar monitor that can
provide continuous, high-quality aerosol data. This monitor will enable us to
better understand and model the complex Earth atmosphere, as well as make more
accurate predictions for the next generation of solar energy forecasting initiatives. This work is dedicated to Prof. Juan L. Cervantes and Prof. Shunichi Fukuchi. We generate synthetic spectra for the TW Hydrae system by simulating the properties of its young stellar object and surrounding disk at different distances from the star. We calculate the H$_2$ emission lines produced by a disk with a mass accretion rate of $10^{-8}$ M$_\odot$yr$^{-1}$ and a wind mass loss rate of either 10$^{-8}$ or 10$^{-5}$ M$_\odot$yr$^{-1}$ due to either photoevaporation or MHD disk wind processes. We consider two scenarios: one in which the disk is smooth and the other featuring a gap at a distance of 30 AU from the star. By analyzing the H$_2$ emission line profiles at various distances from the star and at wavelengths of 1 mm and 0.87 mm, we find that the models without a disk wind or photoevaporation yield more compact emission profiles, while the gap in the disk structure produces more extended profiles. However, this effect is largely obscured by the models featuring a disk wind or photoevaporation. At a distance of 30 AU from the star, the models with a disk wind or photoevaporation produce more extended H$_2$ emission line profiles compared to the smooth disk model, with a difference of up to 50%. This difference is attributed to the disk holes created by both a disk wind and photoevaporation, with a disk wind resulting in more extensive effects. Additionally, the models with a disk wind or photoevaporation produce more powerful H$_2$ emission line flux compared to the smooth disk model, with a difference of up to 100%. This difference is attributed to the disk wind or photoevaporation processes that lead to the production of more free-falling gas far from the star. Finally, the models with a disk wind or photoevaporation yield H$_2$ emission line profiles with a power index that varies depending on the distance from the star, whereas the smooth disk model produces a power index close to 2. automatically extracting fundamental frequency from speech signals without
requiring labeled data. The proposed system utilizes mel-frequency cepstral
coefficients and mel-scale log-frequency short-time spectra features, which
are then compared using a simplified similarity measure. The results are transformed
into probability values. A combination of these probabilities and the speech
signal's energy level are used to determine the mode, while a novel frequency
tracking approach is employed for accurate pitch detection. The method was
evaluated using the Kappa metric on two distinct datasets: the TIDST database and
the WSJ dataset, yielding excellent results, particularly on the TIDST database. A
step-by-step demonstration of the algorithm's operation is available online. The
code has been made available for public access through the https://github.com/
mohamed-abdelmohsen/Automatic-Voice-Activity-Detection.git repository. The
implementation details and the TIDST dataset used for evaluation can also be
found on this platform. The method was found to be highly reliable, with a kappa

parameter optimization technique using the shogun library was employed to select
the most suitable parameters for the proposed algorithm. The research also
involved analyzing the performance of various feature extraction methods and
different classifiers to determine the most effective combination. A novel
technique using a forward-backward Kalman filter was also developed for pitch

By combining the Forward-Backward algorithm with a dynamically adjusted weighting system and utilizing the properties of the Julia constant, the researchers demonstrate that DWIFOB generates sequences that converge to a solution with an optimal rate. Furthermore, the algorithm's design allows for the sequence's convergence without requiring the computation of proximal operators, making it suitable for large-scale applications. The study also provides a convergence analysis for the sequences generated by DWIFOB and shows that, under certain conditions, the rate of convergence asymptotically approaches the optimal rate. To validate the algorithm's performance, the researchers also conduct numerical experiments on real-world image processing and signal recovery problems. The results show that DWIFOB not only achieves a higher rate of convergence but also exhibits a faster iteration pace compared to other algorithms. We have completed a comprehensive one-loop analysis of the neutral Higgs sector in the non-minimal extension of the minimal supersymmetric standard model, incorporating the interaction of a singlet Higgs field with three heavy sterile neutrinos within the type-I framework. Our results correct the Higgs mass predictions, rendering them more accurate, especially for certain NMSSM scenarios. Given the presence of the R-symmetric terms, the r-parameter significantly impacts the Higgs spectrum, causing the CP-Odd Higgs (Pseudoscalar) field to become lighter, which in turn affects the one-loop corrections. Consequently, the light CP-Odd Higgs field's interactions with fermions intensify, resulting in substantial corrections to the Higgs masses. Notably, the corrections are substantial when the intermediate mass scale of the sterile neutrinos is introduced, causing some of the Higgs masses to increase or decrease by an order of magnitude. Moreover, we analyzed various loop corrections in three distinct scenarios, namely when the lightest neutralino is the Dark Matter candidate, where the CP-Odd Higgs acts as a mediator between neutralinos and the Dark Matter is composed of a mixture of bino and wino. In this case, the loop-corrected mass of the CP-Odd Higgs is in agreement with experimental constraints, thereby validating the use of tree-level results for a specific range of values. However, when the light CP-Odd Higgs is within the LHC search range, the loop corrections become substantial, rendering the use of tree-level results inadequate. Lastly, when the light CP-Odd Higgs is outside the LHC search range, the loop corrections become substantial, especially for a specific range of r-values, thereby making the use of tree-level results inaccurate. Ultimately, the choice of model depends on whether the light CP-Odd Higgs mass is derived from the singlet or doublet sectors, thereby influencing the model's viability based on Higgs sector corrections. Moreover, introducing the sterile neutrinos' mass scale within the model causes the CP-Odd Higgs to become soluble, thereby rendering the model's neutral Higgs sector solvable. Lastly, the model is consistent with the constraints of electric neutrality and dark matter abundance. Therefore, the model remains consistent with the Higgs properties and is also in agreement with additional low-energy experiments. Consequently, the model's consistency is confirmed based on the Higgs sector corrections. Moreover, the model's parameter space is constrained by the Higgs production rate in the CMS experiment. Automatically discovering effective neural networks has gained significant interest due to its potential to surpass human limitations in creating architectures. Numerous approaches have been tried, including clever initializations, clever regularization, and the use of evolutionary algorithms, all aiming to reduce the complexity of neural network design. Our approach differs from these previous attempts by employing a different mindset, focusing on developing a synthesis tool that an expert has full control over. Instead of aiming to maximize a specific objective, our goal is to create a neural architecture that exhibits desired properties, such as being suitable for deployment on low-power devices. To achieve this, we developed a language to describe neural architectures and aReasoner to identify the benefits of these architectures. The synthesis tool, guided by theReasoner, enables us to create architectures that outperform previously known and effectively deployable architectures, such as MobileNet, in terms of inference efficiency while maintaining decent accuracy. Our approach also enables the creation of architectures that excel in specific workloads while maintaining a strong overall performance. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the potential of neural architecture synthesis by an expert and provides valuable insights into the relationship between the structure of neural networks and their behavior. Our methodology is available for public use at https://github.com/quantum-ai/neurosynth. A detailed description of our research can be found in the paper titled 'Neural Architecture Exploration using Property Guided Synthesis', published in the Conference of the Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Additionally, our results are presented at the Conference of the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. We are proud to say that our research was supported by the AI Strategic Alliance. We are also grateful for the support of the Natural Science and Engineering Research Council and the Quebec Government's funding through the Fonds de recherche du Quebec - Nature et Technologies. Lastly, we appreciate the support of the IBM Quantum Research Institute. Please feel free to reach out to me at yaochen.zeng@mcgill.ca for further information on how to collaborate with our research. His research focuses on developing innovative synthesis methods for artificial intelligence and neural networks. Prior to his research, he worked as a software engineer at Huawei Technologies and obtained his Bachelor's degree from Wuhan University. We are based at McGill University, 1205 Avenue of the Hill, Suite 1000, Montreal, Quebec, Canada, and can be reached at yaochen.zeng@mcgill.ca.

In this paper, we explore the efficiency of various encoding methods for delivering information to multiple groups in millimeter wave systems. To increase data transmission efficiency in these systems, we can utilize techniques like spatial precoding and encode different data groups separately to avoid interference. However, traditional encoding methods like QAM may not be optimal due to their inability to combat interference effectively. We therefore propose a hybrid encoding approach that combines PM and QAM, allowing for greater versatility and interference resistance. By comparing this hybrid encoding with alternative schemes, such as multi-carrier QAM and multi-carrier PM, we demonstrate the hybrid approach's capacity to provide better performance and greater flexibility in terms of carrier number and bandwidth. Specifically, the hybrid encoding approach yields a greater minimum distance between signal constellations and thus a lower error rate, particularly in systems with a limited number of carriers. Furthermore, this hybrid approach can maintain its advantage even in systems with a large number of carriers, provided the bandwidth is relatively small. When the available bandwidth is extensive, however, the hybrid approach's performance may be comparable to that of multi-carrier PM due to the increased impact of interference. Consequently, we recommend using the hybrid approach for low-bandwidth applications, while switching to multi-carrier PM when dealing with wide bandwidths. Our simulation results align with these recommendations and showcase the hybrid approach's superior performance across a range of scenarios. Ultimately, this hybrid approach enables more efficient communication with lower error rates and thus has the potential to improve the efficiency and reliability of mmWave systems. Specifically, this hybrid approach could be particularly useful in various applications such as 5G wireless communication, satellite communication, and radar, where spatial multiplexing is commonly employed. Additionally, this hybrid approach can be extended to support simultaneous communication with multiple groups while ensuring interference-free transmission. This study presents a novel, communication-efficient approach to distributed training, specifically suited for complex deep learning models and high-speed connection environments. Our technique draws on the principles of Federated Learning, but due to the latency issues associated with synchronizing model parameters across devices, it often proves impractical for certain applications. To address this problem, we introduce a new, efficient protocol for the synchronized extraction of neural network weights from a central server to client devices, and corresponding weight updates from clients to the server. Our model extraction protocol leverages the sparsity of weight matrices in deep learning models, allowing for compression of this data using the Bittorrent Algorithm. Our approach not only minimizes the required data transmission bandwidth but also optimizes transmission data, resulting in a substantial reduction of communication latency and data transmission volumes. Our model efficiency is demonstrated through a series of experiments using the CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets on various distributed computing setups, where we successfully replicate the results of models trained locally on these datasets, with only a minimal increase in computation time. The source code for our model is freely available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/alexanderweinberger/FEEDBACK. Our approach has the potential to enable the widespread adoption of Federated Learning in a variety of real-world applications. Our model also serves as a general framework, allowing for the integration of various learning methods and optimization algorithms. As such, we anticipate that our results will contribute meaningfully to the ongoing research in this field. Our approach can be adapted for other distributed training methods, such as Distributed and Decentralized Learning, where model extraction presents a significant bottleneck to performance. Consequently, our work has the potential to broaden the reach of these methods into a wider array of applications. Moreover, our model enables the efficient computation of per-layer gradient statistics, allowing for the integration of external special hardware, such as specialized GPU or TPU units, for improved performance. Ultimately, our approach offers a versatile solution for the efficient distributed training of deep learning models, where complex computational structures pose significant obstacles to performance. Our model offers a flexible framework that can be adapted for various research domains, such as computer vision, natural language processing, and more. Furthermore, our approach has real-world applications in mobile networks and could be used to develop more efficient learning systems for multiple applications. Our model also enables the integration of research methods from other domains, such as control theory, for example. A key feature of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to facilitate efficient computing services over networks through reverse path forwarding. This capability makes it an attractive option for delivering computing services in NDN-based networks. However, the success of these services relies on the network's ability to provide sufficient quality of service, particularly when dealing with intense traffic and limited network resources. To address this challenge, a new approach called Optimal Dynamic Coordination (ODC) is proposed. By integrating control and data planes through a new module, called the information exchange module, ODC ensures that NDN-based networks can effectively manage bursty traffic and ensure smooth service delivery, as demonstrated using a flow control mechanism in a video streaming application. The benefits of this approach include improved network response time, increased service availability, and better overall quality of experience for users. The proposed mechanism was evaluated through simulations and showed significant performance gains over traditional NDN-based networks. Specifically, results revealed a 69% reduction in packet loss, a 64% decrease in queuing delay, and a 30% improvement in response time. The proposed ODC mechanism is considered general and can be adapted for use in various NDN-based computing services. The validation of this approach using a real-world testbed also confirmed the accuracy of the simulation outcomes and demonstrated the mechanism's effectiveness in managing network resources and ensuring seamless service delivery. The integration of the information exchange module was shown to be capable of detecting and mitigating traffic spikes, thus ensuring the optimal management of network resources and ensuring the optimal quality of experience for users. The proposed mechanism was able to improve network performance by reducing packet loss, queuing delay, and response time. The results of the simulation and real-world testing validate the mechanism's ability to ensure the optimal quality of experience for users and demonstrate the mechanism's generalizability for use in various NDN-based computing services. This study explores the distinctiveness, reliability, and consistency of signature biometrics captured through electronic devices, focusing on the variability introduced by different writing instruments. Our investigation utilizes a diverse signature dataset obtained from various groups, including a group signing their names as instructed, and two groups signing with their actual names in a natural manner. Our analysis evaluates the uniqueness of each group's signatures, the level of variability caused by different writing instruments, and the consistency within repeated signature attempts. Furthermore, our research reveals that the instructed signature group is the most resistant to instrument-based variability and showcases consistent repeated attempts. While NLP can greatly benefit from improved code-mixing handling, existing systems face significant obstacles due to a lack of standardized writing systems, limited resources, and the inherent ambiguity of code-mixing data. It also highlights potential solutions, such as the application of deep learning models, enhanced translation methods, and the optimization of corpus processing techniques. Additionally, the paper discusses the societal implications of NLP in multilingual settings and the need to develop more practical and effective solutions. Finally, the paper outlines potential future research directions and highlights the significant potential of NLP in addressing real-world issues in these societies. Overall, the paper offers a comprehensive analysis of the complexities and challenges of NLP in multilingual societies and the necessary code-mixing handling capabilities. It also proposes strategic research focus areas to tackle these challenges and develop more practical and effective solutions. In the biomedical sector, graph depiction is utilized to convey biological networks such as protein interactions, gene relationships, and disease-associated entities in a visually appealing and easily comprehensible manner. Graph depiction serves several purposes, including data communication, team collaboration, and engaging stakeholders. Nonetheless, the time-consuming and labor-intensive process of manually creating graph depictions makes them inaccessible for various applications. To address this challenge, an automated approach called graph depiction learning is employed, which leverages machine learning to generate graph depictions based on expert annotations. This approach offers several benefits over traditional manual methods, encompassing elevated efficiency, increased scalability, and enhanced flexibility. This review provides an overview of graph depiction learning and its applications in biomedicine, highlighting both the successes and obstacles in this domain. The discussion also explores the potential research avenues and suggests the development of specialized biomedical datasets as a crucial step towards advancing graph depiction learning. The review concludes by emphasizing the necessity of standardizing benchmarks to guarantee fair evaluations and promote consistent progress across the field. The associated resources, including the code and the biomedical graph depiction benchmark, are publicly accessible at https://github.com/AIR-Bayesian-Networks/gdl_benchmark. We examine various models that conceal the pure state nature of a quantum system, which remains mixed even when measured. Our analysis focuses on two types of models: one where a single impurity causes mixed states and another with multiple sources of mixed states. We investigate the uniqueness of these models and their potential to be empirically distinguished. In the singular impurity model, adding more subsystems for measurement purposes doesn't improve understanding of the pure state, whereas in the multi-source model, doing so does. However, both models share a common issue with empirical differentiation. We also explore possible natural constraints on these concealment models arising from measurement limitations and find that they can't fully conceal the pure state unless certain problematic limitations are imposed. Finally, our discussion touches on the broader implications for our understanding of quantum state measurement and the underlying physical world. We also consider whether these types of models could exist in a quantum double-scale universe where a distinction exists between large and small scales. But for now, we leave this possibility for future exploration. Instead, we conclude by highlighting an interesting property that these types of concealment models have in common with certain forms of quantum superdeterminism. In a study of the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, the fragmentation properties of charged particles in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions were investigated. Protons were created from 2015 and 2018 data, totaling 4.1 microbarns of luminosity, and lead-lead events came from 2015 data with 0.4 microbarns of luminosity. The investigation looked at the mean number of charged particles, the particle multiplicity distribution, and the average transverse momentum of these particles in jets with different origins and in conditions of zero, rapidity, and centrality. Observations showed that charged particles in lead-lead collisions had lower multiplicity, shorter particle lists, and lower transverse momenta than proton-proton collisions, and this effect increased as the collision became more central. However, the data agreed with theoretical models and there was no evidence of changes in the fragmentation process due to the formation of a quark-gluon plasma. Additionally, the data were compared to the fragmentation function of isolated photons, showing agreement with expectations, and a study of the angular correlations of charged particles found no evidence of changes in the jet structure in lead-lead collisions. The data were also used to determine the energy density and the pressure of the hot medium created by the lead nuclei. The findings were presented and interpreted in the context of perturbative quantum chromodynamics and its extensions. The analysis included the use of the event-averaged hydrodynamics of the QGP, applying for the last 10-40% of the most central collisions, and the application of Monte Carlo models simulating the action of the parton medium and the effects of interactions between partons and the medium. The data were also used to determine the energy loss of partons as a function of rapidity and the length of the path that partons travel in the medium. The findings were presented and interpreted in the context of models based on the coherence of parton loss. The data were also used to determine the effects of interactions between partons that travel in opposite directions on their energy loss, showing agreement with the idea that partons interact with the medium only once, regardless of direction. The analysis included the use of models based on the idea of parton interactions in pairs (parton interaction mechanisms) and the application of event-by-event analysis to determine the effects of collisions on the behavior of partons. The investigation of solar coronal magnetic fields relies on the observation of small-scale intense X-ray emissions originating from the solar upper atmosphere. These tiny bright X-ray emissions are produced by reconnection events driven by the coronal magnetic field's dynamics. The observation of such emissions allows for the estimation of the coronal magnetic field density. A key challenge is differentiating between the faint X-ray emissions and the background noise observed in space-based measurements. The observation of solar X-rays with the Focusing Optics X-ray Solar Imager is crucial in addressing this limitation as it can directly detect these faint emissions in the frequency range of 5-20 keV. In our study, we analyze the images captured by the multi-layered telescope on board the FOXSI flight experiment during its third flight in 2016. The images exhibit a range of small and intense sources matching the characteristics of solar coronal bright points. The distribution of their counts is consistent with the Poisson distribution, indicating that they represent genuine solar X-ray emissions. The locations of these sources correspond to active regions on the solar surface. Our analysis also shows that these sources are faint, with rates less than 0.1 counts per second per pixel. The detection of these sources enables us to confirm the effectiveness of the FOXSI mission in observing the faintest intense X-ray emissions on the sun. The rates of these emissions are found to be directly linked to the active regions on the sun, leading to higher rates during periods of increased solar activity. The observation of these small and intense X-ray emissions using the FOXSI mission is pivotal in furthering our understanding of the coronal magnetic field density. The results from our analysis are consistent with the predictions of the scenario in which the coronal magnetic field density is controlled by the dynamo process. The success of the FOXSI mission in detecting these faint X-ray emissions has paved the way for the development of future solar missions, including the Wide-field X-ray Imaging Telescope. The latter mission is designed to observe the broad spatial distribution of these faint X-ray emissions across the entire solar coronal area. TheWXIT mission will utilize a large format CCD camera to capture the images of these faint X-ray emissions, thereby enabling precise measurements of their rates and providing crucial data to validate the coronal magnetic field density model. The development of theWXIT mission will significantly contribute to our understanding of the coronal magnetic field density, ultimately enabling us to make accurate predictions of the coronal heating rate based on the dynamo process. Our research focuses on a universe comprising two or more temperatures, where the concept of heat is divided into separate, unconnected aspects. This occurs when the heat in each sector cannot be transferred to the others. Within each individual temperature sector, all matter shares the same thermal energy. GitHub's file system allows multiple versions of the same file to exist based on repository modifications over time. While this feature is beneficial, analyzing the evolution of files across various versions is often challenging due to the lack of a standard approach. To address this issue, we propose a modular and flexible framework called Meta-Maintenance that can leverage the information of shared files across commits to support maintenance decisions. By applying a meta-maintenance strategy, maintainers can tailor their decisions to specific files, commit messages, and maintenance goals, and even replicate the strategies of others for comparative purposes. To demonstrate the effectiveness of Meta-Maintenance, we conducted an in-depth case study on 14 popular open-source GitHub repositories from the Java ecosystem, showcasing its applicability and benefits. Furthermore, we provide Meta-Maintenance as an open-source tool for the community to explore and reproduce our results. Additionally, we suggest several areas for further research based on the diverse characteristics of the analyzed repositories. All our data and results are accessible at \url{https://dm-dk.github.io/MetaMM}.

We introduce a multi-step approach to tackle complex control problems that pose a challenge to traditional deep reinforcement learning methods due to their long time horizons. Our strategy involves dividing the problem into two distinct phases. In the first stage, we use a reinforcement learning algorithm to obtain optimal long-term policies, and in the second stage, we apply these policies to generate shorter-term actions that are easier to learn. Our two-stage method can build upon existing long-term planning techniques, and we enhance it with a short-term reinforcement learning algorithm. Through theoretical analysis, we confirm the effectiveness of our architecture and present experimental results that demonstrate its superiority over traditional deep reinforcement learning methods. Our approach has been successfully tested in two difficult control problems - a simple navigation task and managing power grids - and shows significant performance improvements. Notably, in the power grid management problem, the two-stage method allows for the creation of a reliable and predictable scheduling system. Our work contributes to the development of more robust and efficient deep reinforcement learning algorithms. The code for our approach is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ranar-tecsru-tl-ll/TS-DRL.

This paper is the second in a series exploring the development of black holes through cosmic time, focusing on how massive black holes, including those at the high end, came into existence. Previous research had indicated that supermassive black holes could not have formed through the merger of stellar-mass black holes, due to the lack of nearby mergers in the early universe. A different explanation is offered in this series of papers, which suggests that both large and small black holes arise from distinct formation processes. The current paper specifically examines how massive black holes, including those at the high end, came into existence, particularly through a previously outlined theoretical framework for their creation, as introduced in the first paper in the series. According to this framework, all black holes, from stellar to supermassive, are produced through the same mechanism involving the collapse of dense objects, as supported by recent observations of the growth of black holes. Theoretical models based on this framework are used to analyze data on black hole populations across various cosmic eras, including the early days of the universe, and it is found that this approach accurately predicts the observed patterns of black hole development without the need for separate seeding mechanisms for supermassive black holes, as had been previously thought necessary. This paper reviews the history and changes in the preprints system during this period. Key factors contributing to preprints' success include improved networking, increased user-friendly interfaces, the standardization of metadata, the creation of a unified citation protocol, and the emergence of major preprints platforms, particularly arXiv, which has played a crucial role in physics research. Our analysis reveals that preprints have become an essential part of the research workflow. Based on our study of ten fields, including biology and neuroscience, we find that the preprints ecosystem is dynamic and adaptable. However, the diversity of fields requires varied preprints services. To better serve authors and readers, preprints platforms must be tailored to the distinct needs of each field. To this end, we propose the development of a preprints discovery engine that leverages advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence and deep learning, to help readers discover and navigate the complex preprints ecosystem more effectively. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), characterized by multiple principal components and random atomic arrangements, are pushing the boundaries of traditional materials science concepts. With their unique properties of large entropy and exceptional combinations of mechanical properties, these alloys are gaining significant attention as they can exhibit enhanced strength, corrosion resistance, and unique magnetic properties. As these materials have yet to be fully integrated into real-world applications, computational tools such as machine learning (ML) models are being leveraged to accelerate the design of new HEAs with targeted properties. This article summarizes the current state of HEA research, the potential of ML algorithms in materials science, and their recent integration to design new materials. It also discusses ongoing challenges and offers future perspectives on utilizing ML models to develop innovative materials, including the need for (i) increasing training data, (ii) developing theory-informed models using ML, and (iii) applying ML models to design materials with tailored functionality and accessibility through simple recipe formulas. By harnessing the power of ML, researchers can significantly speed up the materials development process, enabling the rapid creation of novel high-entropy materials with exceptional properties. This article aims to provide an accessible overview of the current state-of-the-art in ML-based HEA design to inspire interdisciplinary research and advance the field of materials science. This knowledge can also be applied to other areas of science and engineering. Additionally, our work highlights the potential of ML not just as a design tool, but also as an analytical instrument to gain deeper insights into the underlying physical mechanisms of materials behavior. This understanding can lead to groundbreaking breakthroughs in materials science and technology. Finally, this article also emphasizes the need to develop transparent and reproducible ML pipelines that incorporate theoretical and experimental findings from the entire community to ensure that the computational tools are indeed reliable and useful. This will enable the seamless integration of ML models into materials design and research, allowing us to accurately predict and develop new materials with unprecedented properties. This knowledge can then be used to develop innovative materials with superior performance, ultimately driving technological advancements and economic growth. This article aims to inspire and facilitate this collaborative effort. This enables us to leverage the full potential of ML and make informed, data-driven decisions to design and develop new high-entropy materials with targeted properties. This knowledge can also be applied to other areas of science and engineering to find novel solutions with significant economic, social, and environmental impacts. This includes developing materials for biomedical applications, such as designing new biomaterials with anti-corrosion and anti-inflammatory properties to replace damaged or diseased tissues in the human body.

To compensate for this, researchers restore the PSF (often referred to as the transfer function or deconvolution kernel) or directly address its effects on the image. Our work focuses on a restoration approach and provides an expression for restoring the PSF under nonlinear response, enabling a more efficient method than previously published algorithms. We then derive an algorithm to update the restored PSF efficiently, allowing the technique to be applied to more images. Our approach is flexible and can be applied to various image combinations, including linear and nonlinear cases. Our method is also adaptable to dimension-reduced image combinations and can be used for 3D image restoration. We evaluate the technique by comparing it with other methods and demonstrating its effectiveness through a range of experiments, including synthetic and real data. Ultimately, our approach enables faster restoration of the PSF, making it more suitable for observational data. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/andrewef/RestorePSF. The subordination technique, initially developed by Lawler and Marmiglio and further refined by Miller and Sheffield, has become a powerful method in conformal field theory. This article explores an application of this approach to the context of the Gaussian free field and multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution. By starting with a random potential of the Gaussian free field on a domain with multiple boundary points, we establish that its level set curve, characterized by a specific transverse deviation, corresponds to the trace of an independent Schramm-Loewner evolution, while the inverse image of a level set also corresponds to the chordal version of the Schramm-Loewner evolution. This article further investigates the relationship between the multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution and the stochastic log-gas, a model driven by a random potential of the Gaussian free field, revealing a natural duality between these two theories. This relationship is substantiated by an explicit example, demonstrating that the boundaries of the domains of the Schramm-Loewner evolutions are all connected to the natural geometric markings of the torus and Klein surface. However, modeling the complex and varied forms of living cells remains a significant challenge due to their intricate shapes and the limited availability of relevant data. To address this issue, we propose a new implicit neural representation approach that uses a low-dimensional latent space to model cell shapes and a conditional normalizing flow to generate cell images based on this representation. Our approach allows us to use conditional convolutional neural networks to capture the relationship between the latent space and image features. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method using the CellAtlas dataset, which contains over 7 million cell images, and find that it produces higher-quality synthetic cell images while also enabling faster training and generalization. Our results demonstrate that our approach can generate synthetic cell images that are comparable to real images in terms of their shape and appearance. Additionally, we find that the latent space encodes information about the type of cell and the viewing direction, which is essential for effective image segmentation. These findings provide evidence that our implicit neural representation framework can be employed in a range of applications in biology and that synthetic cell images can be employed as a useful tool. Our study draws inspiration from reinforcement learning to gain insight into how animals' spatial perceptions develop. Reinforcement learning involves an agent making incremental adjustments to achieve a predetermined goal based on feedback. This process can be challenging due to the exploration-exploitation dilemma, where the agent must balance prioritizing what will lead to success in the long run (exploration) or focusing on the sure things (exploitation). A key question is how animals' spatial maps are refined to represent the long-term goals accurately. Research has shown that rats navigating a maze can learn to associate spatial locations with rewards, but the underlying spatial representation remains unclear. A theory suggests that the representation is initially coarse and becomes more detailed with experience, resembling a scaling transformation. This process bears resemblance to the emergence of precise spatial maps in animals, such as mice, which rely on accurate spatial representations for navigation. To investigate further, we employed a simulation where an agent navigates a grid-world to collect food while avoiding obstacles. The agent's spatial representation is initially coarse and becomes more detailed as it collects food, resulting in a precise map that helps it find the food efficiently. Our findings suggest that the agent's spatial representation is affected by the food's location, its navigation method, and its error history, which can lead to either exploratory or exploitative decisions. A biological representation similar to ours could explain the development of spatial maps in animals, such as the maps generated by neural networks, and provide insight into the underlying mechanisms of spatial learning and memory. Moreover, it can be applied to tackle complex challenges in reinforcement learning, such as achieving long-term goals and balancing exploration and exploitation. Ultimately, the lessons learned can be utilized to develop novel therapeutic strategies for spatial learning and memory disorders. Concurrent transmission in wireless communication systems enables information transfer through multiple entities at the same time, achieving higher capacities and efficiencies by leveraging space, frequency, time, and other resources. This approach uses concepts like superposition coding (SPC) to organize data streams according to users' distinct characteristics and the available resources. As a key enabler for efficient transmission, SPC along with other techniques like beamforming and multi-user MIMO has transformed the field, empowering applications like simultaneous wireless transmission (SWT) with reliable performance. SWT systems, which can transfer information in parallel while maintaining low error rates, rely heavily on effective beamforming and resource allocation strategies. This paper delves into these topics and their control methods, while also exploring deep learning alternatives for improved performance and simpler implementation. Additionally, we discuss the current state of implementation in available hardware and future research avenues for readers to pursue. Finally, we outline various applications across which this knowledge can be applied, including but not limited to, IoT, vehicular communication, and aerial vehicles. By compiling existing knowledge on concurrent transmission and providing a unified framework, this survey aims to contribute to the development of innovative research projects. Its content is expected to benefit advanced students and serve as a valuable resource for academics and industry professionals. Implementation details are also provided for those looking to bring these concepts to life in practical projects. This comprehensive survey first reviews the fundamental principles behind concurrent transmission and superposition, before moving on to explore beamforming techniques and innovative deep learning methods for enhanced performance. Next, it discusses the practical implementation of these concepts, followed by a look at various applications across which this knowledge can be applied, and finally concludes with suggestions on how to approach research projects in this field. Due to the extensive literature on this topic, we have standardized our approach by only considering the most influential papers and providing brief summaries for each section, while also making the primary sources readily available for further reading. Time-stamped spectral measurements, known as spectrograms, are often obtained from signals with significant gaps in frequency domains, typically associated with notable changes or events within the signal's sequence history. These gaps appear as level sets within three-dimensional plots, where the remaining spectral values form continuous regions. We investigate these regions as continuous, smooth areas in a two-dimensional surface, using techniques from modern stochastic analysis to develop a theoretical framework for measuring their properties, such as connectivity and dimensionality, and the flow of intrinsic differential forms, all at a level of precision applicable to practical signal processing. This framework is applied to the detection and characterization of frequency jumps in spectrograms, along with estimating the jump's occurrence time and a measure of its magnitude. The method is further developed to detect multiple jumps by jointly analyzing the spectrogram's level sets across a time window, where the detection of jump instances is treated as a sub-problem of finding critical points within this combined surface. Finally, we present a practical implementation of these methods, along with corresponding numerical tests that validate their effectiveness, revealing improvements over existing jump-detection methods, particularly in situations with limited post-jump spectral observation. Additionally, we discuss the broad applicability of these methods to general level sets, along with their potential applications across various fields. We introduce a novel approach for detecting chimera states, comprising of a chimeric network's stable and synchronized components, using a measure called chimera quantity (CQ). This measure effectively captures the chimeric structure by measuring asynchrony within subgroups and intra-group coherence. It can detect chimera states in various forms, such as spatially extended and fragmented configurations. The CQ measure possesses several advantages, including robustness to parameter changes, ease of computation, and ability to identify chimera states in networks with hidden chimera states. Additionally, it can track the evolution of chimera states over time and even pinpoint the emergence point. Numerical simulations demonstrate the CQ measure's efficacy in different network scenarios, such as a ring network with non-locally coupled inhibitory and excitatory interactions, and an incomplete lattice network featuring non-locally coupled excitatory interactions. The CQ measure has the potential to be adaptable to various complex network topologies, making it a valuable tool for scientists. The code used to generate the results is available upon request. It also includes a user-friendly interface and pre-written code to make it accessible to a broad audience. The package was tested on different systems and is now available for download at the mentioned repository. To analyze the stability of planetary systems, researchers employ N-body simulations, which model the gravitational interactions among celestial bodies with high precision. However, these simulations typically assume deterministic gravitational forces, overlooking the potential impact of stochastic forces, which are significant in certain astrophysical contexts. This study aims to adapt the REBOUND N-body code to include stochastic forces, leveraging them to generate new types of orbits. Two novel features have been added: firstly, the code can alternate between active and inactive states, based on a random driver that simulates a stochastic force, potentially leading to planetary ejections; secondly, the integration path can be perturbed, inspired by Lévy flights, resulting in a spiral pattern of motion. Our modifications enable researchers to model planetary ejections and alter the motion patterns in N-body systems, offering fresh avenues for investigation. This research explores the idea of creating a blocked disk setup with two different sized disks in a channel, focusing on arranging the disks using a repeating sequence of weights. The study reveals that using this repeating sequence approach, nearly all possible weight configurations can be achieved, with only a limited set of weights inaccessible. Specifically, if the channel's width $N$ is comprised of multiple $M$-wide segments where $2M$ is less than or equal to the smaller disk's diameter, the resulting weights mod $N$ are restricted from $0$ to $M-1$. Notably, when the larger disk's diameter is equal to $L+2M$, the resulting weights mod $N$ are further restricted to $0$ to $L+M-1$. Consequently, when $L+M$ is less than or equal to the smaller disk's diameter, the only achievable weight is $0$. Furthermore, when $L+2M$ is greater than the larger disk's diameter, the achievable weights mod $N$ are essentially unrestricted. Building upon this concept, a theoretical model has been formulated, which uses a combination of different weights to determine the number of achievable weights mod $N$. The model's results are then compared with previously established findings on using a single type of weights, which also leads to some interesting conclusions and open questions. Additionally, some examples have been provided to visually demonstrate the concept and illustrate some of the paper's key findings. Lastly, some potential applications and related research areas have been highlighted, which could further expand our understanding of the underlying mathematical concepts. Ultimately, this research contributes to the ongoing exploration of using blocked disks to arrange objects in a channel, using a sequence of weights, which has exciting implications for further investigation.

By employing cross-correlation analysis and machine learning techniques, the focus is on determining whether stock time series is in a state of synchronization. An efficient method called the Dynamic Time Warped Distance is developed to calculate optimal lag parameters for cross-correlation, which in turn informs the selection of stock price samples for classification. Additionally, the study employs two new indices: the Center Cross Density and the Concentration Index, to enhance classification performance. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of these indices and a Support Vector Machine classifier in achieving a 90% accuracy rate for a one-step prediction horizon. Furthermore, an investigation into feature selection strategies reveals that Random Forest, a feature selection method, generates outcomes comparable to those of the proposed approach. Consequently, a SVM classifier utilizing the proposed time series samples, derived from the proposed indices and lag parameters, is recommended for predicting synchronization in stock time series. An application of the method is also provided for the S&P 500 index components, showcasing its practical utility. The acceleration of a particle generates vibrations in the associated crystal lattice, resulting in electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions that are influenced by the particle's momentum. Using a general approach, we derive analytical expressions for these interactions in the context of 2D materials. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed analysis of the electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions within the specific examples of MoS2 and WSe2, and explore their magnetic properties under the influence of phonons. Our findings demonstrate that the momentum of the particle indeed plays a significant role in determining the strength of these interactions, particularly in the spin channel. Moreover, we derive a condition that must be satisfied for the spin channel to be influenced by the particle's momentum. Our research also reveals that the magnetic field can either amplify or diminish the effects of the electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions, depending on the material's type. To confirm our theoretical predictions, we perform extensive computational simulations using density functional theory and the Hubbard model. Our research lays the groundwork for a broader understanding of the electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions, ultimately contributing to the development of more accurate models for describing these phenomena. Additionally, we identify a significant application of these interactions, namely their potential to modulate the spin polarization in 2D materials, thereby enabling the creation of spin-based devices with self-circulating currents at room temperature. Our research also opens up the possibility of employing momentum-accelerated phonons to control the spin, a concept known as "spin-orbit-phonon" that could have a significant impact on the development of advanced spintronics and quantum technologies. To facilitate experimental investigations of these interactions, we outline specific procedures for measuring their effects, such as by creating ultra-thin 2D samples with uniform phonon characteristics. Our research paves the way for the development of innovative spin-based devices, where the unique interplay between phonons, spin, and momentum is harnessed to produce robust spin polarization at room temperature. Ultimately, our analytical expressions and theoretical predictions could be applied to a range of 2D materials with magnetic properties, thereby expanding our understanding of the complex behavior of these materials at the atomic level. Finally, we note that our theoretical model can be adapted for use in various 2D materials by replacing the Hamiltonian with one that is relevant to the specific device under consideration. To facilitate the replication of our research, we outline specific steps that can be taken to build upon our theoretical model and experimental approaches.

Current click-through rate (CTR) prediction models are primarily based on user behavior data and ignore the essential characteristics of promotional content. As a result, when encountering unfamiliar ads, models perform poorly. To address this issue, our proposal shifts the focus from solely user behavior to also incorporating visual elements commonly found in ads. Not only do visual elements provide valuable information about ads, but they also significantly influence users' click behaviors. However, directly incorporating visual features into the model is impractical due to the varying sizes of ad distribution pools. To resolve this problem, we divide the vision module into two components, one that extracts and one that processes features. The former module converts ads into unified feature sets, while the second module leverages the power of language models to extract critical information. From extensive experiments on industrial datasets, our proposed model has demonstrated superior performance, with a 6.8% improvement in overall accuracy and a 8.6% improvement in new-ad CTR prediction when compared to the baseline model. Notably, our model has outperformed state-of-the-art models by 3.6% in overall accuracy and 4.1% in new-ad CTR prediction. Furthermore, our model has exhibited impressive generalization capabilities, with a 1.7% increase in new-ad CTR prediction while maintaining comparable performance on established ads. Uncontrolled wildfires disrupting air travel due to ash contamination, causing flight cancellations and delays, leads to significant economic losses. To rectect this impact, a system is needed that can accurately detect and track wildfire-induced ash clouds and predict their likely progression, thereby enabling timely decision-making for air travel management. Achieving this requires integrating multi-source satellite remote sensing data and incorporating physical laws that govern the movement of ash particles, heat transfer, and fluid dynamics. Specifically, a physics-based statistical learning approach is developed and demonstrated using geostationary satellite imagery, resulting in a method that can effectively capture the dynamics of ash cloud behavior while accounting for variable atmospheric conditions and the temperature dependencies of ash particles, as evidenced by a successful case study in California, USA. The developed procedure is validated by comparing its predictions with actual ash cloud observations, revealing a high degree of consistency and accuracy. Moreover, the system is capable of providing a predictive outlook, with positive results. Furthermore, the system's ability to model ash cloud behavior under different conditions is demonstrated by conducting a series of experiments, including changing the initial and boundary conditions. Additionally, the system is utilized to estimate the impact of air and ash particle density, as well as the ash particle size and shape, using in-situ measurements and computational fluid dynamic simulations, with the resulting predictions showing a high degree of agreement. The proposed procedure is considered an essential step towards developing an air-quality forecasting system that can effectively utilize available satellite data in an intelligent and automated manner. The ultimate outcome will be a system that can provide accurate ash cloud predictions, thereby minimizing the economic impacts of flight disruptions. The detailed procedure is now available for public use, enabling other researchers and developers to replicate and modify the approach for their specific applications. The system's source code, including the Python algorithms, as well as the required satellite data and parameters, are all freely accessible and can be adapted for other applications, including air quality monitoring and wildfire management. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of multivariate approaches in multisite generalization and functional connectivity-based prediction. Building on previous work by Dong and Song, we demonstrate that a directed graph with non-negative Ricci curvature exhibits exponential heat diffusion convergence and a concentration of measure property. Additionally, we derive new inequalities for directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature and establish a directed graph analog of the Bakry-Émery Ricci curvature formula. This results in a novel characterization of positive Ricci curvature through a inequality involving the graph's spectral gap. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a directed graph with non-negative Ricci curvature and almost identical transition probabilities for each vertex can be transformed into a metric measure space with a lower bound on its Ricci curvature. Finally, we prove that such a directed graph exhibits exponential heat diffusion convergence and a concentration of measure property. This research provides insights into the relationship between a directed graph's curvature and its transition probabilities. Recent breakthroughs in NLP research enabled code-mixed documents to be processed by Automatic Identification Systems, but data availability for these languages is severely limited, making development of these systems particularly challenging. To address this issue, this research aims to develop an adaptable encoding technique for code-mixed texts, allowing its effective application across various language pairs. To this end, a novel positional encoding method, called PESTO, is proposed, based on switching points identifying different language segments within a sentence. PESTO employs two PESTOs, one for each language, using a relative position encoding technique that leverages the sequential relationship between language segments. Comparative experiments with existing solutions and alternative approaches were conducted, yielding PESTO's superiority in several key areas, along with the open-sourced code and the CSTCorpus dataset for further research. CSTCorpus was created by combining datasets from Mexico and India, totaling 23,537 annotated instances, which can be accessed via a custom-built web interface for easy exploration. PESTO's efficiency and generalizability were demonstrated by its successful application on two distinct tasks, using a pre-trained model and a simple classifier, respectively. Notably, the best results were achieved using PESTO's output as the sole feature. Building on PESTO, several variants of the positional encoding technique were explored, along with the potential for its integration with other Positional Encoding methods. A thorough analysis of the findings, along with the direction for future research, is also provided. Ultimately, PESTO provides a viable solution to the data scarcity issue and facilitates the development of new systems using the CSTCorpus dataset and the CSTCorpus web interface. Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations, we analyzed the electronic structure and superconducting properties of the H$_3$S hydride as a function of pressure. Along with this, we examined how the density of states affects the isotope effect and critical temperature as pressure increases. Our results indicate that the critical temperature of H$_3$S hydride under pressure follows an exponential trend, and that its isotope effect decreases under pressure, eventually becoming negative at higher pressures. This behavior can be attributed to the increasing influence of the van Hove singularity in the density of states, which is accelerated by pressure and causes a sharp peak in the density of states. This peak significantly affects the electron-phonon interaction and the superconducting properties of H$_3$S, leading to the observed decline in isotope effect and the potential for achieving ultra-high critical temperatures above 260 K under pressure. However, our calculations also reveal that the critical temperatures predicted by the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer and Migdal-Eliashberg models differ substantially, underscoring the importance of considering strong coupling effects in analyzing superconducting properties. Moreover, our findings suggest that the origin of the unusual pressure dependence of the isotope effect of hydrogen sulfide can be attributed to the presence of the van Hove singularity. Finally, our research paves the way for the exploration of new superconducting materials containing sulfur or selenium, and the potential for achieving ultra-high critical temperatures in these materials through a sulfur or selenium-based hydride or amide compound. Additionally, our results can guide experimental investigations of the isotope effect and the optimization of pressure for achieving the highest possible critical temperatures in these superconducting materials. Overall, our research highlights the pivotal role of the van Hove singularity in the superconducting properties of H$_3$S hydride and the need to consider its influence in analyzing the electron-phonon interaction and the superconducting behavior of sulfur-based hydride superconductors. Moreover, our results can guide the development of new high-temperature superconductors based on main group elements. Finally, our research demonstrates the significance of strong coupling effects in analyzing superconducting properties, particularly in cases involving strong electron-phonon coupling and high critical temperatures. Additionally, our results can facilitate the development of more accurate theoretical models for predicting superconducting properties, particularly those that take into account the influence of van Hove singularities and strong coupling

Fisher designed an experiment to illustrate the difference between two statistical concepts, the average effect and the finite population correlation. His intention was to demonstrate that these measures are distinct, yet he inadvertently made an error that has been corrected, revealing that the average effect actually mirrors the finite population correlation when the variables are paired randomly. Furthermore, this equivalence serves as the foundation for Fisher's original finding that the average effect is the optimal estimator of the finite population correlation. Notably, the correlation coefficient can be calculated as the average effect when the variables are paired nonrandomly, drawing a connection between Fisher's work and the principles of causal inference outlined by Pearson and Tukey. The latter posited that the Pearson correlation coefficient represents the causal effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable when the variables are paired nonrandomly. In this context, the Pearson correlation coefficient can be reinterpreted as a measure of the causal significance of the independent variable, where the variables are paired nonrandomly according to the underlying mechanism governing their relationship. Consequently, the distinction between correlation and causation that has long bedeviled the scientific community may be a product of the ambiguous language used to describe statistical concepts, rather than any inherent complexity. When a central server and multiple clients engage in federated learning, differences in client data distributions can cause performance disparities after the model has converged. Introducing semi-supervised learning can enhance overall efficiency, but the limited availability of labeled data and variation in local data distributions pose significant challenges. To address these issues, we develop a novel approach called Personalized Federated Semi-Supervised Learning (PFSSL). The central server estimates the correlation between classes and the client-specific ambiguity, then guides the local model updates with customized techniques tailored to each client's data distribution. Our framework comprises three main components: 1) a unified model shared among clients and the server; 2) the server calculating class correlation and ambiguity for each client, with optional regularization; and 3) a decentralized algorithm for optimizing the shared model. Our approach is implemented using three distinct local optimization methods: 1) a two-flow algorithm with forward and backward propagation; 2) a modified PSGD method; and 3) a combination of FedAdam and AiryGaussian. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed framework yields better performance and reduced performance gaps compared to existing solutions. Furthermore, our study highlights the significant impact of variation in data distributions on model performance and the importance of considering personalized factors. Our code is publicly available for review. Additionally, our results show that our framework can achieve comparable performance to that of models trained on a homogenous dataset, while using a shared model and decentralized algorithm minimizes communication requirements. Our study also reveals that FedAdam and AiryGaussian outperform other optimization methods in terms of efficiency and convergence speed. Our proposed framework and associated results demonstrate the importance of considering personal factors and ambiguity in federated semi-supervised learning, ultimately leading to improved model performance and reduced communication requirements. Our findings have potential applications in various domains, such as mobile and distributed computing systems. Our study also sheds light on the novel challenges arising from data distribution variations and labeled data scarcity in Federated Learning, and provides a framework to address these issues. Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted to obtain a comprehensive picture of the inspiral, merger, and post-merger stages.  The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals a uniform sequence of events, regardless of setup variations.  The system evolves through an initial mass-aspiration phase, followed by a disk accretion phase characterized by magnetohydrodynamic turbulence and radiation-driven fragmentation, then enters a quasi-steady state.  The duration of this fragmentation phase spans 3-13 seconds, influenced by equations of state for neutron stars, initial magnetic field strength, and field configuration.  The instability grows within 1-3 seconds, producing a central low-entropy envelope surrounded by a radiation-driven fragmentated disk.  The initial fragmentation phase is followed by a period of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence with a magnetic energy comparable to the kinetic energy of the accretion flow, lasting between 6 and 30 seconds, depending on the simulation.  The structure of the accretion flow and the fragmentation phase undergo minimal changes after 20-40 seconds and remains relatively stable for the duration of the simulations.  The final mass distribution of the system is consistent across the configurations, featuring a black hole of mass 1.20 solar masses, surrounded by a disk of approximately 0.036 solar masses, and a neutron star remnant whose mass depends on the equation of state for neutron stars.  The disk mass is independent of the initial magnetic field, but influenced by the equation of state for neutron stars, resulting in a 30% variation.  The models with stiff equations of state for neutron stars tend to experience less fragmentation and weaker magnetic fields in the disk, while those with softer equations of state for neutron stars experience more fragmentation and stronger magnetic fields in the disk. To understand patterns in treatment durations at hospitals, we've developed a mathematical approach using average curves for analysis. This method allows us to analyze treatment times at various points in time, using a framework similar to stochastic processes. Our approach uses average curves derived from reference distributions and weighs them by the probability of those times occurring. This approach differs from traditional Markov process analysis, which may not accurately represent the beginning or end of treatment periods. Our method is demonstrated through a case study of an emergency department (ED), where we define treatment as the period between an patient being assigned to a room and the completion of care. Specifically, we analyze the average treatment duration curve (ATDC) and the probability density function (PDF) to understand treatment durations. Our study of a large hospital reveals that the ATDC and PDF near the start of the treatment period are quite different from each other, highlighting the importance of considering the initial treatment phase separately. Our mathematical framework provides a useful tool for understanding and improving emergency healthcare services. Furthermore, this method enables the calculation of key performance indicators, such as the average treatment duration and the standard treatment duration, in addition to the ATDC and PDF. By investigating the origins of a long queue in the ED using our method, we identify the underlying cause and make recommendations for changes to the hospital's treatment process. Our analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of creating a treatment room from an emergency care unit to reduce the length of the queue and improve patient satisfaction. We investigate the cooperative efforts of multiple robots working on different tasks while also competing with one another to complete their assigned jobs quickly. Each robot attempts to do so by simultaneously adjusting its production rates and schedules to align with its competitors', using minimal energy. Our study yields algorithms and strategies that yield strategic, stable equilibrium points in various scenarios, including when the interconnectedness of the robots follows a specific, repetitive pattern. Furthermore, we examine the potential outcomes when the interconnectedness of the robots random in nature. Our analysis reveals that at least one stable equilibrium exists and we develop methods to calculate the others in both the aforementioned scenarios. Moreover, we investigate how the distribution of the interconnectedness of the robots impacts our findings. Our results demonstrate that when the competition is evenly distributed, our algorithms yield a singular stable equilibrium, whereas in cases of uneven distribution of competition, our algorithms yield multiple stable equilibria. Moreover, we show that regular patterns of competition favor cooperation among the tasks. Our work contributes to the body of research on the theory of cooperative games and provides insights into the design of control mechanisms for tasks like demand management in shared networks. Additionally, our study showcases the utility of cooperative game theory in analyzing the behavior of self-interested robots working together to achieve common goals. Our research also highlights the effect of the distribution of competition on the outcome of strategic multi-task synchronization, thereby influencing the design of control mechanisms for shared networks. Moreover, we uncover a connection between the local interactions among the tasks and the global outcome of strategic multi-task synchronization. Our results are validated through simulations using graph theory's small-world model and regular network models. Moreover, we demonstrate the applicability of our findings to the design of a distributed, fast-converging algorithm for shared networks via a simple example. The surge in crowdfunding usage has spawned a corresponding need for a deeper understanding of the crowd dynamics that influence its successful implementation. Our cross-cultural, multi-platform study examines online crowdfunding dynamics by gathering data from over 100 successful fundraising campaigns in Brazil and Italy. By analyzing negative feedback responses from donors, we uncover a distinct temporal pattern in crowd behavior, with implications for a crowdfund's success. Our findings reveal that donor behavior shifts from initial skepticism to heightened engagement over time, with negative feedback serving as a catalyst for increased donations and social connections within the crowdfunding platform. This pattern holds true across different platforms and cultures, and is confirmed through the analysis of quantitative metrics and text related to donor behavior. By providing a quantitative model for predicting fundraising success based on crowd feedback, we contribute to the development of more effective strategies for managing and optimizing crowdfunding campaigns. Ultimately, our research sheds light on the complex, dynamic nature of online crowds and offers a nuanced understanding of the crowd dynamics that shape the outcome of a crowdfund. The analysis of crowd behavior also enables the creation of value in the crowd itself. As such, our work is relevant not only to crowdfunding but also to any online environment where crowd interaction plays a key role in achieving a shared goal. Machine learning (ML) based detection of network attacks has become a widely accepted approach. However, its effectiveness depends on an extensive labeled dataset, which can be difficult and costly to obtain. To address this challenge, research has explored the concept of collaborative machine learning. This study proposes a novel federated learning (FL) framework for an intrusion detection system (IDS) that enables collaboration between multiple institutions. A novel FL mechanism is developed for updating the model and aggregating data. This collaboration enables institutions to share knowledge while maintaining data privacy and avoiding the need for a centralized dataset. Through numerical analysis and two case studies, the generalization performance of the FL-based IDS is demonstrated. Compared to local training and conventional FL, the proposed FL-based IDS exhibits enhanced performance and a broader applicable range. Specifically, the results show that the FL-based IDS achieves a 44.97% improvement in accuracy for the 198.44.1-16 dataset and a 27.94% improvement for the NSL-KDD dataset, with a training loss reduced by 85%. Furthermore, the FL-based IDS is found to be more robust and adaptable than traditional ML-based IDS methods. Notably, the model can be updated with new data without requiring re-initialization, showcasing the advantages of FL for cyber threat intelligence sharing. This novel FL framework thus offers a practical and effective solution for institutions to collaborate in developing an intrusion detection system while minimizing costs. The proposed framework may also be applied to other domains beyond cyber security. The source code for the FL-based IDS framework is publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/zhenghui2019/FederatedLearning.git. This public repository can be utilized by researchers and practitioners for replicating the experimental results and further developing FL-based applications. Moreover, a cloud-based testbed has been established at https://cyber-physical-systems.github.io/FL-based-IDS for online replication of the experimental results. This testbed can be accessed by users for duplicating the experimental results and verifying the performance of the FL-based IDS under different configurations. To facilitate knowledge sharing among researchers and practitioners, two detailed tutorial papers have been published, which are available on arXiv at the following links: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.09075 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.06530.
