The problem of scheduling a robot's tasks is a well-defined problem with a proven polynomial solution method, which we call the Task Robot Problem (TRP). The key challenge in TRP is assigning a specific time frame to each task so that each task is completed by a robot at the appointed time. The tasks must be completed within predetermined time limits to ensure that each robot has sufficient processing capacity and time to complete the assigned tasks. In the optimal TRP solution approach, a bipartite graph is initially established to represent task-robot relationships, where edges represent the time it takes for each task to be completed by each robot. The graph is then divided into independent groups with minimal time requirements, where each group contains tasks that can be completed by the same robot. The time requirements of these tasks are combined and minimized, resulting in a reduced total time requirement for all tasks. The triangles with the longest edges in each group are identified, where each triangle represents a sequence of three tasks that can be completed by the same robot in a specific order. The worst-case scenario time complexity of this algorithm is proportional to the number of triangles. The algorithm is tested using a dataset of 1000 random tasks, where each task can be completed by one of ten robots with different processing capacities. The results show that the algorithm is efficient, requiring a fraction of a second to complete, and demonstrates good generalization capabilities, where the TRP dataset is expanded to include 3000 tasks and the resulting time requirements are scaled by a factor of 30. The outcomes confirm that the algorithm is scalable, where the total number of tasks can be completed in less than 30 milliseconds. The algorithm is also compared to other scheduling methods, where the difference in completion time is significantly reduced, and the total time required for task completion is minimized, resulting in a 26.7% reduction of the optimal TRP solution approach and a 35.1% reduction of another scheduling method. The efficiency of the algorithm is further confirmed by analyzing its time and space complexities, where the total number of tasks and the number of robots are the critical parameters. The algorithm is finally evaluated using a real-world robot manipulation sequence, where the outcomes demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of the algorithm in scheduling tasks for multi-point robotic manipulation. Our study examines the existence of source variety bias in video search outcomes, where a particular field or domain influences the video source platform's bias. We suggest a method of auditing this bias by pretending to be a video uploader and requesting the removal of a video due to copyright infringement. By sending removal requests to major platforms such as YouTube, Vimeo, and Dailymotion, and tracking their responses, we are able to gauge the diversity of fields represented in their databases. Our survey of over 35 fields across three countries reveals that while YouTube receives copyright infringement claims from a wide range of fields, its actual database may lack variety in fields like fine arts, whereas Dailymotion's database may be more diverse but with a higher likelihood of biases being overlooked. Furthermore, our analysis of response times across different fields shows that fields like finance receive responses within minutes, whereas fields like fine arts take over a month to receive a response. Our findings suggest that while some video platforms may claim to have a comprehensive collection, their actual variety is limited and this poses challenges for both researchers and developers. We propose possible solutions, such as using source variety bias to improve AI models, exploring underrepresented fields in data collection, and developing more effective methods of auditing bias. Our code and data are publicly available for reproduction of our results. We believe that our research can contribute to a better understanding of the diversity in video search databases and its implications for both the video search and computer vision communities. We hope that our work will inspire more research into this area and facilitate the development of more diverse video databases for both research and development purposes. We envision a future where video search databases are more comprehensive and diverse, meeting the needs of users across a wide range of fields and domains. We plan to present our findings at relevant conferences and research meetings to disseminate our research and foster collaboration. To address this shortcoming, we propose a new approach where we assign different weights to nodes based on their potential contribution to the prediction. This approach is further validated in two practical scenarios involving energy-harvesting capabilities in single- and dual-user networks. Accurate tracking of mobile devices' locations is a critical requirement for numerous applications across various sectors, hence reliable mobile localization techniques are essential. In environments where GPS signals are obstructed or have low reception rates, alternative technologies such as radio-based localization utilizing Wi-Fi or cellular networks become vital. A widely employed method for achieving high precision in these environments is Positioning Data Assortment (PDA) algorithm. Our research reveals that the standard PDA algorithm is susceptible to signal outages and can yield suboptimal results. To address this issue, we introduce an Adaptive PDA (APDA) algorithm that adjusts its approach based on the availability of signal data. During periods of signal presence, the APDA operates similarly to the original PDA, leveraging Deep Neural Network (DNN) predictions to maximize data utilization. When signal outages occur, the APDA shifts to a predictive technique to minimize location tracking disruptions. Our simulation outcomes and real-world experiments demonstrate that the APDA algorithm offers superior performance and robustness compared to the standard PDA algorithm, particularly in scenarios with signal outages. Furthermore, the APDA is shown to be more efficient and accurate than other mobile localization techniques such as Deep Learning-based methods. Our findings indicate that the APDA maintains a low error rate for both large and small signal outage durations, thus maintaining consistent performance across different environments. To facilitate seamless integration with existing systems, the APDA can function as a sub-module within deeper mobile localization architectures. Ultimately, the APDA can be integrated into various positioning systems as a standalone module to deliver enhanced mobile localization and tracking capabilities. Our proposed APDA algorithm is adaptable to various use cases such as cellular network-based localization, Wi-Fi based indoor localization, or combined cellular and Wi-Fi outdoor/indoor localization. To showcase the APDA's versatility, we also present a case study on combined cellular and Wi-Fi outdoor/indoor localization, which highlights the algorithm's ability to provide a seamless and continuous quality of service in mixed outdoor and indoor settings. To demonstrate the APDA's capabilities in real-world environments, we also conduct a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance in a publicly available dataset, the Wi-Fi dataset from UCSD, which showcases the APDA's ability to provide accurate indoor localization results while navigating through the campus. Our analysis reveals that the APDA is capable of providing a high level of precision in real-time while accurately determining the mobile device's indoor location. To validate the APDA's performance in a real-world setting, we also conducted a field experiment on a bus route

This paper proposes a monitoring method for hybrid process models defined by both flow-oriented and one-way branching transitions, expressed using conditions based on time and past events. The aim is to identify violations of temporal constraints related to event occurrences, taking into account the model's timeline and event history. The monitoring method involves constructing a specific automaton, which is then used to determine if a given process alignment with the model represents a feasible or infeasible scenario. The model can be represented in either (i) a flow-oriented or (ii) a hierarchical and compositionally structured format. In both cases, the primary focus is on detecting when a process deviates from a viable timeline. In case of a deviation, the monitoring method is enhanced to identify the first point of incompatibility between the process's progression and the model's transition requirements. The proposed monitoring approach relies on an automaton built with three types of transitions: time advancements, event recognitions, and condition-based decision points. The paper outlines the automaton's construction and presents two algorithms for calculating the model's timeline and event history. The monitoring efficiency is then compared with alternative methods on sets of randomly generated hybrid models. The paper also explores the relationship between model complexity and monitoring performance. Finally, the monitoring results are presented in relation to the model's structure, which allows for the development of a method to quickly identify infeasible scenarios and provides a measure of infeasibility for each process step. This study addresses the text-to-SQL semantic interpretation challenge in natural language processing. Most current methods focus on learning database schema and table relationships from labeled data, but this is inefficient as modifying the schema requires retraining the model. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that does not rely on labeled data for table relationships. Instead, we leverage the knowledge of column names and can adapt to new schema elements with only unlabeled data. To achieve this, we employ a dual-module network that combines column and row information to interpret SQL. The row module can be optimized without labeled data for table relationships by cross-lingally transferring knowledge from questions in zero-shot settings. To further enhance our model, we introduce an auxiliary task, generating column names, which bridges the gap between column and row representations. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our model, and it demonstrates greater flexibility and adaptability compared to existing methods. Notably, it can effectively handle various database schema without labeled data for table relationships and can interpret SQL without seeing the full table structure. Moreover, it can generate more accurate column names and translate better to row information. Overall, our model offers a more efficient and scalable solution for text-to-SQL semantic interpretation. The code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/whaiwhai/CDTSIQ/tree/master.

We refer to a class of problems known as stacking problems, where each input object can be decomposed into simpler components through the application of a given set of transformation rules. These problems are defined across three distinct domains: algebra, logic, and recursion. Notable examples include solving polynomial equations or determining the validity of first-order logic formulas with specific parameters. A key concept in studying these problems involves kernelization, which enables the reduction of a given instance to a more manageable version while preserving its solvability. Building on existing kernelization techniques for specific stacking problems, we develop more general kernelization procedures applicable to the broader class of stacking problems. This achievement is grounded in a novel algebraic characterization of these problems, which reveals the essential role of commutative, associative, and closure properties in facilitating kernelization. Consequently, this advancement allows for the creation of tighter kernel sizes and more efficient kernelization outcomes for individual problem instances. Furthermore, our findings are illustrated through the application of our kernelization procedures to previously intractable instances of algebraic and logical stacking problems. Ultimately, this research contributes new insights into the complexities of these problems, thereby expanding our understanding of their theoretical constraints. The study of web studies relies heavily on the assumption that a comprehensive search covers all relevant information. However, the impact of personalized search results on the validity of this assumption has never been scientifically examined until now. This study investigates the extent of relevant information that may be missed due to customized searches by analyzing the characteristics of non-personalized Google searches. Our findings reveal that about 12% of necessary information is likely overlooked. The analysis also shows that the amount of information that may be missed more than triples when the search query is related to sensitive topics. This amount remains steady across various levels of online content diversity. Our hypothesis suggests that the amount of information that may be missed could increase if customized searches become even more precise. This potential bias could significantly influence the outcome of web studies, particularly those focusing on delicate topics. To address this limitation, researchers should employ alternative search engines like DuckDuckGo that do not personalize results to ensure more comprehensive data coverage. Past attempts have focused on the cell-based approach, where each cell represents a program statement or value, and the flow of data between cells corresponds to program execution. The proposed GRCNN approach distinguishes itself from existing solutions by introducing two key contributions: (1) a graph recognition module that filters out irrelevant cells, ensuring the program structure is accurately captured, and (2) a flow-type aware module that incorporates temporal relationships between cells, enabling the generation of coherent program behaviors. The GRCNN approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a remarkable 88% matching accuracy and an impressive 93% overall generation score. The proposed methodology is thoroughly detailed, along with empirical evidence and insights obtained during evaluation. The found results indicate that GRCNN generates program graphs that closely mirror the original flow chart, with an impressive overall generation score. The generated programs are also evaluated using the metric of semantic similarity, revealing a substantial 41.2% boost in performance. The empirical evaluation validates the efficacy of the proposed GRCNN approach, establishing it as a leading method for program generation from flow chart representations. Our study focuses on employing deep learning techniques to automate segmentation of the gastrointestinal tract in CT images for patients with ascites. Furthermore, our approach also exhibits improved accuracy when compared to other segmentation techniques, demonstrating the efficacy of anatomic prior-based segmentation. Additionally, our method demonstrates robustness to ascetic distortions and its ability to operate effectively in the absence of the GI tract. The extensive HARPS and CORALIE radial velocity surveys have uncovered numerous exoplanets, offering valuable insights into planetary mass distribution below a saturation threshold where multiple-planet systems may potentially harbor planets similar in size to Earth or larger in mass, such as Jupiter. To investigate this, we analyzed a sample of 115 planetary systems from these surveys, focusing on those featuring a single known planet and no evidence of additional planets. We selected 13 planets with a 3-year radial velocity constraint period and a host star age less than 10 billion years, then applied a statistical model to assess the likelihood of additional planets in these systems. Planets with a 3-year constraint period and a mass ratio greater than 0.1 were found to have a 95% probability of hosting an additional planet with a similar mass ratio. However, for planets below this mass ratio threshold, the probability dropped to 57%. Our analysis indicates that roughly half of the planets in our sample could potentially host an additional sub-Saturn mass planet based on current evidence. Furthermore, we discovered that detecting additional planets in our sample would require a radial velocity detection limit below 10 Earth masses per square second or a Gemini or ELT telescope. In summary, our findings reveal that numerous planetary systems in our sample can accommodate additional planets, highlighting the significance of follow-up observations to uncover these missing planets and gain a more comprehensive understanding of the mass distribution in exoplanet systems. Our analysis also has implications for characterizing habitable zone planetary systems, suggesting that these systems are more likely to harbor additional planets, including those with masses similar to that of Jupiter. In the context of the TESI project, our analysis paves the way for identifying and characterizing additional planets in these systems using wide-field spectrographs. In particular, targeting specific follow-up candidates could facilitate the detection of super-Earth or Neptune-mass planets that could significantly advance our understanding of these planetary objects. Our analysis also explored the potential of direct imaging and found that it is not a viable method for detecting additional planets in our sample, except in specific cases where the separation between the planets is relatively large and the mass ratio is substantial. However, direct imaging may be effective in detecting additional planets with large separations, such as those in the HD 69830 and HD 219449 systems. Our analysis also examined the potential of transit photometry and found that it is not suitable for detecting additional planets in our sample, except in specific cases such as HD 69830. In many complex situations, relevant information within an agent's perception is difficult to pinpoint.  Agents like humans, successfully filter out unimportant details by focusing on elements that greatly impact their goals.  This ability is exemplified in humans through attention control, while advanced machine learning agents lack this capability, relying on attention mechanisms designed externally which may not be adaptable in dynamic environments.  This study presents a novel approach where an uncontrolled attention source and a goal are linked tightly together, resulting in the agent prioritizing information that is most beneficial to goal achievement.  We implement this approach using a mutually informative generative adversarial network and demonstrate its effectiveness in comparison to traditional attention mechanisms on two tasks: navigation in a simulated maze and remote driving image classification.  The results show that the method is highly adaptable and difficult to manipulate by adversarial attacks, indicating that the model is controlling attention effectively.  Moreover, this approach results in better attention allocation and more robust performance across various levels of adversarial interference. We revisit traditional global pooling techniques in neural networks in the context of optimal transport. By doing so, we develop a new global pooling layer based on a novel solution to a previously unsolved problem in optimal transport research. Our approach has the added benefit of allowing for the computation of a pooling layer for more than just two networks, which is essential for applications such as domain adaptation. Furthermore, we extend this method to unsupervised domain adaptation tasks involving multiple domainers, and our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this layer in several such scenarios. Our research also connects global pooling to a broader framework of functional maps, which we use to create multiple domainers for a given task. Additionally, we find that global pooling can be applied to other machine learning models that employ element-wise operations beyond neural networks. Overall, we believe that future research on optimal transport should focus on developing more customizable and flexible global pooling layers. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

The growing family of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) classifies the core subcategories known as Radio Galaxies (RGa), Quasars (Q), and Low-Ionization Metal-Oxygen Absorption Line (LIMOST) Galaxies. Our investigation contrasts the host galaxies of these distinct AGN types, focusing particularly on their morphological structures, star formations, and the AGN's inclination relative to the stellar disk. Our analysis leverages high-resolution images from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Spitzer Space Telescope to study the host galaxies of 83 RGa, 52 Q, and 52 LIMOST Galaxies within the z = 1.5-2.3 redshift range. Our findings reveal that RGa are predominantly found in massive, structured host galaxies with twisted radio jets, low star formation rates, and the AGN positioned at the center of the host. In stark contrast, Q and LIMOST Galaxies reside in less massive hosts with lower morphological complexity, increased star formation rates, and the AGN often offset from the host's center. Furthermore, the offset ratio between the AGN and the host's center significantly differs, with negative values indicating the AGN is actually within a central cavity created by the AGN's jets, a characteristic almost exclusive to RGa. Our research demonstrates that the host galaxies of RGa, Q, and LIMOST Galaxies significantly differ based on their morphological structures, star formations, and the AGN's orientation relative to the host. These distinctions imply that the AGN feedback played a crucial role in shaping the host galaxy's structure, particularly in the RGa system. Ultimately, our research highlights the distinct life cycles of RGa, Q, and LIMOST Galaxies, with the RGa phase characterized by powerful radio jets, massive host galaxies with twisted structures, and the AGN positioned at the center. These distinct phases are separated by a distinct "quasar mode" during the RGa phase, marked by significant star formation suppression and efficient AGN feedback. This quasar mode is absent in the Q phase, where the AGN power is largely unregulated by surrounding matter. During this time, the AGN either actively drives the host galaxy's evolution or is surrounded by a neutral, star-forming cloud that prevents AGN feedback. Our research also resolves the long-standing enigma surrounding the "quasar mode" and the AGN-IGM feedback, revealing a distinct "quasar mode" characterized by powerful radio jets

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort.
Pre-training with a vast amount of image data can alleviate this burden by leveraging a standard supervised learning task, such as image classification. Recent research has explored using depth estimation as an alternative for pre-training, asserting that multi-task learning with segmentation and depth estimation can boost accuracy and efficiency. Conversely, we argue that depth estimation might not necessarily enhance training, and instead, propose that its effectiveness depends on the specific network architecture and training methods used. We demonstrate that, in certain situations, pre-training with image classification is more beneficial, and highlight the influence of the chosen task for pre-training on the final performance of the model. We also examine the potential of using depth estimation for pre-training in detail, and find that it is largely dependent on the quality of the estimated depths, rather than an inherent advantage. Furthermore, we investigate alternative approaches for pre-training, including unsupervised depth estimation methods, and evaluate the performance of three such techniques, which we found to be inferior to classification-based pre-training. Ultimately, we recommend utilizing existing supervision from the target dataset, and provide guidance on the integration of unsupervised pre-training methods for pre-trained models that lack sufficient supervision. Our experimental setup and source code are publicly available, allowing for replication of the results. We also offer an open-source pre-trained model for unsupervised pre-training, which can be adapted to various tasks and domains. Creating engaging audio content involves adding voiceovers to explain and provide context for data such as financial reports, sports statistics, or location history. While current approaches focus on translation and domain-specific narration, resulting in stories often filled with unnecessary words like "last month" or "yesterday" that fail to convey action and interest. To address this, we introduce TCube, a translation and narration framework that can explain time-series data in a variety of domains without requiring knowledge of a specific domain. TCube uses a neural model to generate narratives by analyzing temporal relationships and incorporating temporal expressions in a more engaging manner. Our experiments, conducted across three domains with both English and Chinese as the languages, demonstrate that TCube surpasses leading translation and narration tools, producing narratives up to 14% shorter while retaining 95% of the original information and receiving 25% to 41% more positive human feedback compared to a 1.4% difference in the baseline. Additionally, TCube is capable of explaining data in spoken form, enabling it to outperform other explanation methods and a GPT-powered model. By adjusting learning rates and incorporating robust error handling, this network has achieved exceptional results on challenging datasets, including the top-1 accuracy record in image classification, demonstrating its potential for widespread application in devices. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Traditional implementations rely on each party sending their parameters to a central point, but this can be insecure due to potential data exposure in the central location. To address this, we present an anonymous federated learning framework that employs homogeneous models across parties and only allows the shared vector to be updated. This approach, combined with techniques such as vector blending, enables efficient model updates without revealing individual data. Furthermore, we integrate this framework with two distinct forms of secure multi-party computation: homomorphic encryption and oblivious transfer, to create the Flatee system. This system allows parties to collaborate while isolating each other, using either remote or local connections. It also includes a secure administrator, responsible for overseeing the training process. We evaluate Flatee's performance against recent systems and find it to be more efficient on various datasets. Specifically, it achieves a 38.4% reduction in communication cost and a 57.1% decrease in computation overhead compared to the Axop system. In the realm of containerized microservices, achieving optimal performance and efficient resource usage can be complex, especially considering the various configuration options available. For example, when a web server within a container makes a system call to create a socket, it may either use the socket library directly or through a proxy like Apache Traffic Server, necessitating multiple system calls. To address these issues and allow the system call sequence based on application behavior, we present a method of learning system call policies through automated analysis. By employing the Salsa library to generate system call graphs and identify program invariants, we can model a microservice's behavior and determine the optimal system call sequence. Our approach allows for policy learning and adapts to changes when the code is modified, as seen with the evaluation of a web server and a database. Furthermore, we show the efficiency of this method by comparing it to traditional manual configuration, revealing a significant reduction in processing time and increased resource usage with our approach. Ultimately, we believe that our method enables the efficient and efficient deployment of microservices by learning and optimizing system call policies. To facilitate this, we provide a tool called Timeloops that can learn these policies and demonstrate its value through several examples and configurations. To the best of our knowledge, this method of learning system call policies for containerized microservices has not been explored previously in existing research. Our future work will focus on integrating this method with existing containerization technologies like Docker and Kubernetes. Additionally, we aim to address the existing limitation of our method not being able to handle concurrent system calls. Nonetheless, we believe that this research will contribute positively to the area of autonomic computing by enabling autonomous system call policy learning for containerized microservices. To facilitate this, we make our tool and methodology available for other researchers and practitioners to reproduce our results and build upon our research. This paper introduces a novel sparse sensing framework known as compressive singular component analysis (cSCA), which aims to identify the primary components of a given data set through minimal sensing. The methodology involves capturing data subspace information via a few optimized samples and then utilizing this data to estimate the dominant singular values and associated modes. The optimality of the sensing matrix in cSCA is demonstrated through an explicit characterization of the sampling matrix's spectral properties. The challenges posed by the complexity of the cSCA problem are addressed through the development of two iterative algorithms: (i) cSCA using alternating least squares (cSCA-ALS), and (ii) cSCA using alternating least square with reweighting (cSCA2R). The efficacy of these algorithms is substantiated through numerical analyses and a range of experimental results presented in this paper. The cSCA framework holds significant practical value due to its potential to streamline various applications, including hyperspectral imaging and remote sensing, by utilizing the framework's capabilities for sparse spectral analysis. The accompanying appendix provides a comprehensive mathematical framework for the cSCA model and associated algorithms. Furthermore, a corresponding R package has been developed to facilitate the reproduction of the presented results. The package, known as cSCApkg, can be accessed through https://github.com/zhengwuhai/R_cSCA. We have identified a previously unexplored threat where an attacker can manipulate machine learning classifiers by exploiting vulnerabilities in communication channels. This is achieved through the creation of manipulated models that can bypass input validation, allowing the attacker to intercept and modify data in transit. As a result, the attacker can craft malicious inputs that the classifier incorrectly identifies as valid, or alter existing inputs to deceive the classifier. To illustrate this threat, we will describe two examples of vulnerabilities in popular Python frameworks that enable this type of attack, as well as several scenarios involving image and text classifiers that demonstrate our methodology. Furthermore, we will discuss potential countermeasures and outline future areas of research. Interestingly, this threat highlights the fact that the security of machine learning classifiers often relies on the security of the surrounding ecosystem, rather than just the model itself. By exposing this vulnerability, we hope to raise awareness among researchers and practitioners, leading to further investigation and mitigation strategies. Ultimately, this threat serves as a reminder that the security of machine learning systems is a shared responsibility. To quantify the impact of this threat, we will present empirical evidence of successful attacks against various machine learning classifiers, as well as the corresponding loss rates for each classifier. Notably, some of these attacks have been successfully demonstrated in public demos, highlighting the ease with which attackers can exploit this vulnerability in real-world applications. To facilitate defense against this threat, we will outline several potential countermeasures, including input validation, the use of trusted data sources, and reliance on models that are resistant to manipulation. Additionally, we will discuss the importance of secure communication protocols and regular software updates to prevent exploitation by malicious actors. Finally, we will outline several areas of research that could be undertaken to address this threat, including the development of secure machine learning pipelines, the creation of detectors that can identify manipulated data, and the design of machine learning models that are inherently resistant to manipulation. By exposing this vulnerability, we hope to stimulate research in these areas and drive the development of more secure machine learning systems. Some of the machine learning models used in our study, such as the Adversarial Trained ImageNet model, as well as our custom-generated adversarial examples, can be found on our GitHub repository. Furthermore, we have outlined our methodology for creating malicious generative models, which can be adapted for use in other research projects. By sharing our approach, we hope to facilitate collaboration and help researchers who may be working on related projects. To effectively read ancient documents, their physical state must be improved. The process of document enhancement involves enhancing low-quality images to facilitate better interpretation. While current methods can produce satisfactory results, they often fail to surpass human reading capabilities, particularly for documents with severe damage or those from novice writers. A major limitation of these methods is their narrow focus on text extraction, which overlooks the overall document interpretation. To address this issue, we propose a novel multi-task adversarial network that not only removes external interference but also distills valuable knowledge from high-quality text to enhance low-quality documents. The framework consists of three modules: a text-enhancement block, a text-translation block, and a discriminator. Through extensive experimentation on the TSINGHU, METAR, and NII-EDU for English, Japanese, and Chinese datasets, our model has demonstrated superior performance, achieving a character error rate 7% lower than the existing best methods. The proposed architecture is also adaptable to various document enhancement tasks and can be applied to handwritten documents by integrating an additional feature extraction module. The resulting model exhibits a 3% character error rate reduction. The source code is available at https://github.com/Chen-2022-RTB.

This task is particularly challenging due to its reliance on comprehensive color codes and the need for extensive domain knowledge. Our approach to colorization involves the development of a custom dataset based on the SDSS colorspace and an encoder-decoder model that incorporates residual learning with a generative adversarial network (GAN) for improved performance. By comparing our method to the Colorization2GAN model, which was optimized for the colorspace, we found that our approach achieved better results on the astronomical dataset. Additionally, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our model by applying it to the restoration of historical black and white astronomical images. Our findings reveal that the model successfully reproduces the color characteristics of the original images, thereby enabling the production of high-quality colored images in various colors. Furthermore, the analysis of our results and those of Colorization2GAN suggests that the performance of image colorization models can be enhanced by incorporating knowledge of the specific colorspace in question. Lastly, the application of our model to the restoration of historical images showcases its potential for real-world use in the fields of astrophysics, remote sensing, and cultural heritage preservation. The task of relation extraction has been a major focus for NLP researchers over two decades, with the goal of extracting relevant information from written content. Despite significant advancements, the task remains a challenge due to ambiguous sentence structures and limited context. A new approach combines relation extraction with knowledge graph link prediction to provide additional context, effectively transforming the task into a multiple-choice format. This enhanced framework capitalizes on existing knowledge graphs to offer three feasible outcomes for each extracted relation: the confidence of the relation was increased, the relation could be swapped, or the relation was incorrect. This technique was evaluated on three datasets and compared to four leading models, resulting in improved micro-F1 scores of 2.7%, 8.2%, and 12.1% for the respective datasets. Furthermore, the proposed method demonstrated exceptional performance in handling difficult cases and provided interpretable reasoning output similar to that generated through knowledge graph link prediction. To facilitate future research, the proposed method, along with associated code and datasets, has been made publicly available. This technique has the potential to be integrated with existing NLP models to enhance their performance in relation extraction and related applications. Additionally, the model can be modified to engage in counterfactual reasoning by swapping relations without altering their truthfulness, which could be explored in the foreseeable future. To verify this potential, the model was tested on two datasets and showed a 5.2% improvement in micro-F2 scores, indicating its capacity for advanced, counterfactual reasoning. Consequently, the model can be utilized for the generation of artificial knowledge graphs, thereby driving the development of NLP models that can draw inferences from relationships. This research has the potential to contribute to various real-world applications by demonstrating that NLP models can produce plausible outcomes on real-world data through counterfactual reasoning. This peculiar magnetic configuration is attributed to the irregular distribution of magnetic fields generated by the 4f spins within the material's structure. Crystals of Tb3RuO7, exhibiting a monoclinic crystal system with the P21/m space group, were found to display two unique transitions at 18.5 K and 4.8 K, respectively. Analysis of the material's magnetic properties, using an internal magnetic field simulation in combination with the Monte Carlo method, has provided a comprehensive understanding of the material's magnetic behavior. Our simulation results reveal that the material's magnetic arrangement is partially disordered at 18.5 K, featuring short-range ordering of the 3d spins. Additionally, our findings indicate that the material's magnetic arrangement is highly sensitive to the ratio of the effective magnetic moments of the 3d and 4f elements. This study offers a valuable insight into the material's magnetic behavior and highlights the inherent relationship between the material's magnetic arrangement and its crystal structure. Furthermore, our observation of a partially disordered state in Tb3RuO7 has prompted us to propose a new category of magnetic arrangement, distinct from the paramagnetic and antiferromagnetic configurations. We term this arrangement 'quasi-antiferromagnetic', characterized by the random orientation of spins within planes, while spins between planes are aligned. We anticipate that our observation of this 'quasi-antiferromagnetic' arrangement will serve as a common feature of materials exhibiting magnetic arrangement that is neither paramagnetic nor antiferromagnetic. Furthermore, we provide a mathematical explanation for the model's success, highlighting the importance of causality in generative learning. The Hubbard model, a fundamental quantum lattice system, faces a significant challenge known as the sign problem. This critical issue restricts the range in which wave functions can vary, effectively hindering the convergence to the ground state using traditional algorithms. Historically, various approximations have been employed to overcome this limitation, yet none of these methods have been able to fully eliminate the sign problem. More recently, advancements in complex-valued neural networks have provided hope for a possible remedy. Our study serves as a comprehensive overview of these modern algorithms, while also introducing a novel application to the field, and we rigorously examine their performance in a specific high-energy context. Additionally, we propose a possible solution by utilizing a novel complex-valued neural network, which can mitigate the sign problem to some extent. Our findings demonstrate that this network is capable of approaching the ground state within a specified range of parameters, a feat that was previously considered infeasible. Our study also highlights the potential of integrating these complex-valued neural networks into variational quantum eigenspectroscopy, a quantum algorithm used to find eigenvalues of a molecular Hamiltonian, thus bringing us closer to achieving a breakthrough in this field. Lastly, we introduce a novel approach based on the phase-augmented Hamiltonian, which can partially mitigate the sign problem; this method exhibits significant improvements over existing algorithms, and we provide valuable insights into its potential and limitations. Overall, our study showcases the vast potential of incorporating complex-valued neural networks to overcome the sign problem, thereby enabling the development of more accurate algorithms. Our proposals also offer promising directions for future research and development. Moreover, our study provides a detailed evaluation of the performance of these complex-valued neural networks, thereby establishing a benchmark for future comparisons. Finally, our work culminates in the presentation of a sign-free phase, the long-awaited goal of which holds significant theoretical and practical implications. Our study investigates the influence of head-mounted display distortions on user experience in virtual reality applications. We examined various common distortions such as field of view, resolution, and tracking accuracy, as well as more complex issues like head-to-head alignment and distorted visual perspectives. Our goal was to determine their impact on user performance and level of comfort. We conducted experiments involving a shooting game task to measure performance and a comfort questionnaire survey to gather subjective feedback from participants. Our results show that while some distortions have a significant effect on user experience, others have a negligible impact and surprisingly, in some cases, even improve performance without affecting comfort levels. Interestingly, we found that the optimal range for field of view in our game scenario was actually beyond 110 degrees, while resolution had a more significant impact on performance than field of view. The study also revealed that user comfort and performance were influenced more by system limitations than by field of view or resolution. Our findings provide valuable insights for VR system design and can inform the development of more effective applications, suggesting that the optimal range for several key factors may vary depending on the specific application and use case. We believe that these results will contribute to the advancement of the field and promote the development of more efficient and user-friendly VR technology. Recent high-mass binary system discoveries through microlensing have drawn attention to binary star formation at masses greater than 20 $M_{\odot}$.  Past research has suggested that binary formation is influenced by the way material accretes onto forming stars.  To investigate this, we conducted a study of how a rotating core with an initial mass of 240 $M_{\odot}$ undergoes fragmentation evolves as it gains mass.  Our findings show that when the core's mass grows, it becomes more difficult for its rotational energy to drive motion of mass towards the core's center, thereby reducing effusive accretion and generating a more massive binary system.  As a result, the binary system's mass range in the core's center is anticipated to be wider than in cores with lower rotational energy.  Our simulations' outcomes are consistent with the masses of binary stars observed in the Milky Way.  It is worth noting that when a core's mass grows, its binary system may experience gravitational stripping, which could lead to the formation of smaller systems, such as multiple systems with narrow-separation.  Our work may help to explain the diverse ranges of binary system masses that have been observed. We re-evaluate the capabilities of choiceless polynomial time (CPT) in distinguishing specific graph structures, applying a novel approach that leverages algebraic properties from a recent study. This examination also considers a related but more powerful logic, partiality-sensitive choice polynomial time (PSP). Our study's findings serve as a comprehensive overview on graph distinction within the CPT and PSP frameworks, offering a significant benchmark as a reference point. To gain insight into these frameworks' expressive powers, we compare them with two established propositional satisfiability (SAT) solvers – polynomial calculus and extended polynomial calculus – and introduce a new parameter to gauge their performance. This new parameter, known as the algebraic shift, helps us reflect on recent advancements in the theoretical limits of these solvers. We also utilize this study to outline potential future research directions, including exploring more intricate graph configurations and expanding upon existing distinction results in CPT and PSP. Furthermore, incorporating results from recent experiments in machine learning can facilitate the empirical evaluation of different logic systems, making it an intriguing area of study. Last but not least, we highlight the similarities and differences between logic-based distinction and the algebraic approach of reducing instances to known solvers like XPMC and EPMC. This comparison enables us to apply established results from the study of proof complexity to gain a deeper understanding of the expressive powers of CPT and PSP. To illustrate this connection, we present an algebraic reduction from a graph distinction problem in CPT to an instance in XPMC, and show that this reduction is feasible under a specific condition known as algebraic connectivity. We also examine the distinction of specific graph configurations, particularly odd cycles and certain bipartite structures, and introduce two new notions – local and global polymorphic encodings – to express these graphs in a more flexible way. Our study culminates in a comprehensive comparison between CPT and XPMC, and we identify key distinctions between these two frameworks, ultimately reducing certain graph distinction problems in CPT to instances in EPMC. We also introduce three new parameters to evaluate the complexity of graph distinction problems in CPT. To conclude, we highlight numerous research avenues that remain unexplored and encourage further investigation into these areas. Additionally, we present a detailed outline of our thesis, dividing it into sections and providing relevant results along the way. This outline serves as a valuable resource for obtaining a comprehensive understanding of the subject matter. The growing issue of unfalsifiable claims on social media, which cannot be verified through objective evaluation, has become a major concern as they can rapidly spread and influence a wide audience. These baseless assertions, often made by high-profile individuals, can perpetuate harmful misinformation and erode trust in institutions. To address this, we aim to investigate the underlying structure of unfalsifiable claims by extracting common elements and establishing a framework for categorizing related statements. This initiative has the potential to break down unfalsifiable claims into more manageable components, making them easier to fact-check and counter. By dissecting these claims, we can also identify the sources of misinformation and develop targeted strategies to combat them. Ultimately, our goal is to create a practical approach that can be applied to various domains and help mitigate the spread of unfalsifiable claims. In this paper, we explore two possible frameworks for organizing these claims, one related to conspiracy theories and the other involving false narratives. These frameworks are discussed in more detail, along with their challenges and limitations, as well as potential future research directions. Additionally, we present an interactive visualization of our findings on unfalsifiable claims, showcasing our framework and highlighting areas for further investigation. The accompanying code and visualizations can be accessed through our GitHub repository for reproducibility purposes. This project has been made possible through a collaborative effort involving undergraduate researchers who contributed to this study. We believe that by engaging undergraduate students in this research, we can leverage their knowledge and skills to investigate novel approaches for understanding unfalsifiable claims. This study aims to investigate the dissemination of online rumors in China during the COVID-19 pandemic by developing a novel metric called "Influence of Rumors" (IR). A systematic approach has been devised to analyze the behavior of these rumors by tracking their source, spread rate, peak impact, and extent of dissemination. A numerical model is also proposed to categorize rumors based on their spread rate. A data set consisting of 
$11,799$ rumors was used to test the efficacy of the developed metric, revealing that nearly
$32\%$ of the evaluated rumors met the criteria for analysis. A novel prediction method, called ProCS, has been created to predict the chemical shifts of amide proton chemical shifts in proteins. This method, powered by quantum mechanics, has been shown to be highly accurate and has enabled the development of a quantum-mechanical based refinement tool for protein structure refinement. By comparing predicted and actual chemical shift values in a refined protein structure, ProCS can identify regions where the conformation may be improved. This tool has been successfully used to refine the 1.9 A resolution structure of the B domain of human complement component 1 by refining 102 residues, resulting in a 0.3 ANM score improvement and 14 total distortions in the final model. Additionally, our approach has the potential to be combined with other refinement methods, such as molecular dynamics, to further refine protein structures. ProCS predictions are made using short quantum-mechanical trajectories and are typically completed within a day, even for large protein targets, due to recent advancements that have increased the computational efficiency of the code. This method has been validated through comparisons of various tests and has shown superior performance in chemical shift predictions when compared to other state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, our approach has the potential to be scaled up to include more accurate quantum-mechanical descriptions of protein structures using techniques such as the polarized continuum model for describing environmental effects. Overall, ProCS has been shown to be an efficient and accurate tool for refining protein structures, resulting in improved results when compared to other available methods. Additionally, our approach has the potential to be used in future studies of protein-ligand complexes and other systems. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, yet the underlying reasoning behind this perspective often lacks clarity. In contrast, the relationship between loss functions and final objectives is relatively straightforward in traditional regression and classification tasks. This simplicity motivates this study, which seeks to establish a more detailed understanding of how loss functions influence performance in established classification models. To this end, we investigate whether using a sum-of-logs objective (also known as cross-entropy) is equivalent to using the Kullback-Leibler divergence with regularization in terms of its optimization behavior and empirical performance on well-established classification datasets. Our results indicate that these objectives exhibit comparable optimization characteristics and yield similar, albeit minor, performance improvements when employed on modern convolutional neural networks. Notably, our findings suggest that the purported difficulty of optimizing cross-entropy loss with SGD may be an unfounded assumption. Based on these outcomes, we hope to contribute to a more informed discussion regarding loss function selection in deep learning and provide a clearer understanding of the relationship between objectives and loss functions for future researchers to build upon. The code to reproduce our results can be accessed at https://github.com/alexmankiv/loss_functions. Additionally, our pre-trained models can be found on https://github.com/alexmankiv/convnet-pretrained. Emergency dispatchers play a vital role in providing timely assistance and guidance, yet their interactions with callers are often overlooked. This deficiency in information hinders in-depth analysis and improvement of dispatcher-caller relationships. To address this, a text-based reporting system was implemented, allowing the collection of data on dispatcher-caller conversations. This paper examines the characteristics of these conversations, including linguistic features, and reveals a notable disparity in the language used by callers and dispatchers. We introduce a groundbreaking learning framework called Minimax Engaged Learning (MEL), a dynamic interplay of exploration and exploitation that optimizes a game. In this context, the explorer represents our model, and our goal is to minimize the cost of exploring the data landscape. In the initial phase of MEL, the explorer initiates by selecting its most advantageous action based on the game's current state, and then the adversary responds by choosing an action that disrupts the explorer's decision-making process. Subsequently, the explorer learns from this encounter and updates its policy using an actor-critic algorithm, and the cycle repeats until a termination condition is met. Actor exploration mechanisms, such as RND and information-based exploration, can also be integrated into MEL for added diversity. By engaging in this minimax paradigm, MEL enables our model to actively learn from its adversary and achieve superior generalization performance. Notably, our approach exhibits a remarkable reduction in measurement costs compared to conventional exploration methods. Our experiments demonstrate that MEL surpasses several efficient exploration techniques and achieves remarkable results, particularly on the ImageNet dataset where it generalizes exceptionally well to in-plane rotations. Unlike conventional OOD (out-of-distribution) detection methods that broadly categorize data as OOD, this research proposes a more nuanced approach, recognizing two distinct types of OOD data: 1) truly novel data and 2) anticipated data. Novel data is unknown and unrelated to the training dataset, whereas anticipated data is foreseeable and has underlying connections to the training dataset. Building on this understanding, we introduce two criteria for differentiating between these two types of OOD data and present a framework for identifying anticipated data. Notably, our approach to OOD data identification does not rely on model performance assessment but rather explores the concept through in-depth analysis. This research also outlines the implications of our findings and suggests possible applications, such as transferring OOD data handling skills and leveraging OOD data for downstream tasks. Our method is demonstrated using the Converse dataset, a resource that facilitates the exchange between two different languages. Our work offers a new perspective on OOD data and could potentially influence how future research approaches data exploration and analysis. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Our Converse dataset can be accessed through this link: https://github.com/whaiwhai/OOD-Converse/blob/main/converse_dataset.py. It can also be obtained by contacting the research team.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 sparked significant interest, but the spectroscopic features of this cooling object remain shrouded in mystery due to the lack of a suitable model spectrum. By developing a new model using the APOLLO retrieval code, our research provides the first accurate spectrum of GJ 229B, enabling the identification of its composition and thermal evolution. Our model indicates that GJ 229B's atmosphere primarily consists of methane, ammonia, and water, with the ammonia concentration decreasing as the atmosphere cools. The new spectrum reveals signs of water absorption at 1.6 $\mu$m, consistent with this model's predictions. The reconstruction of GJ 229B's thermal evolution reveals a history of significant internal heat production, with the ceasing of this process occurring around 750 million years ago. The resulting thermal timeline is comparable to that of Jupiter and Saturn. The absence of evidence for the presence of phosphorus compounds in GJ 229B's atmosphere suggests these compounds may not be stable in the low-temperature environments of T-dwarfs. The findings of our study provide a framework for the development of a comprehensive model of T-dwarf atmospheric formation, with implications for the study of low-temperature atmospheres. The derived GJ 229B model spectrum is compatible with observations from the Spitzer, Hubble, and Keck telescopes, as well as past thermal evolution studies. The integration of our results with the ExoMast model indicates that GJ 229B should be observable in the near-infrared band with the JWST, making it an attractive target for future spectroscopic studies of T-dwarfs and potential exoplanets. We introduce a concept of double sided auctions with the ability to verify the accuracy of bid and ask price submissions, thereby addressing the issue of malicious activity in such markets. This malicious activity, facilitated by the ability to submit fake bids and asks in the form of false information, leads to overpricing and undervaluing of goods. Through the incorporation of a truth-telling mechanism, we design a new type of auction that not only detects but also penalizes dishonest participants. This auction operates on a regular market schedule, where price adjustments are made in real-time based on the verified bids and asks of participants. Our model is further developed to account for the costs associated with verifying bid and ask accuracy, as well as penalties for dishonest behavior. Using numerical analysis, we demonstrate that increased profits can be gained by participants when the ability to verify bid and ask prices is integrated into the auction system. Additionally, we have found that the losses incurred from penalties for dishonest behavior are minimal. This leads us to the conclusion that the double sided auction with verification is a reliable and efficient market mechanism. Finally, we have conducted an experiment where we have compared regular auctions with penalties for dishonest behavior to those with verification, and found that the latter yields better results. This has potential real-world applications, given the prevalence of auction systems that price goods. These findings indicate that a superfluid with spin singlet nature can arise from both necessary and sufficient conditions for topological superfluidity. Moreover, the topological superfluidity is accompanied by a pair of flat bands located at the Fermi level, comprising electron-like and hole-like states that originate from the spin-dependent nature of Rashba energy levels. These flat bands serve as evidence of spin-orbit coupling in the system. By examining various band structures, the spin-orbit coupling's effects on spin degeneracy can be observed, leading to the conclusion that a strong coupling will result in spin degeneracy elimination. Ultimately, the topological superfluidity and the associated spin degeneracy elimination characteristics of this model make it an ideal candidate for spin-orbit induced superconductivity in 2D systems. Additionally, the model's topological properties can be evaluated through both spin-texture and spin Hall effect analysis, where both properties are found to be present. The spin Hall effect is characterized by the spin current $I_s = \frac{\alpha e}{\hbar} J_\downarrow$ due to the spin-orbit coupling. This study focuses on tabular data found in scientific documents, requiring two key assessments: first, the validation of factual information presented in the tables, and second, the identification of supporting evidence for such facts. To address these challenges, we introduced a new SemEval task known as SEM-TAB-FACTS. In total, we created 5500 annotated tables from 1024 biomedical research papers, with 2700 tables used for training and 1300 tables for testing, and an additional set of 800 tables for development purposes. Three teams took part in the competition, submitting four submissions altogether. Our analyses show that accurately pinpointing the tables, identifying the relevant rows, and validating the facts proves to be complex tasks. Interestingly, two teams managed to surpass the baseline set in the testing phase, with their submissions also demonstrating a high level of agreement among human annotators. This data set and the associated code will be made accessible, enabling future researchers to build upon this work. Building on the success of this task, we plan to refine and expand the data set, and introduce new evaluation metrics to better align with the requirements of the domain experts. Moreover, we will explore the application of more advanced natural language models to tackle these challenges. With a particular emphasis on improving table understanding, we will specifically investigate methods that utilize the table structure itself, and the relationships between different elements within the table. In quantum mechanics, the use of complex numbers for wave functions and operators is a fundamental aspect that has been widely accepted since the early days of this theory. However, the justification for employing complex numbers in quantum mechanics has not been thoroughly explained. We argue that this acceptance stems from a historical compromise made by Paul Dirac due to the limitations of his early relativistic quantum theory, specifically the presence of 'unphysical' solutions in the energy-eigenvalue equation. To overcome this issue, Dirac arbitrarily discarded the 'unphysical' solutions without providing a clear theoretical basis. As a result, the formalism of quantum mechanics appears complicated and inconsistent. We propose a simplified alternative to the Dirac theory, namely the real Klein-Gordon theory, to demonstrate that the necessity of complex numbers in quantum mechanics is a false legacy of the Dirac theory. The real Klein-Gordon theory, developed using real wave functions, can serve as a sufficient model for both non-relativistic quantum mechanics and the electromagnetic Schr\"{o}dinger equation. We further generalize this approach to apply to the electromagnetic Dirac equation, obtaining a real first-order spinor wave function in this process. The derivation of the spin-statistics theorem from the electromagnetic Klein-Gordon and Schr\"{o}dinger theorems, through the proposed generalized approach, remains unaffected. We conclude that the formalism of quantum mechanics is consistent and can be applied using real wave functions and operators. We examine the implications of this conclusion on the mathematical structure of this theory, particularly its signature and metric. We discover that the real wave function satisfies a unique hyperbolic metric, allowing us to explore the topological properties of the configuration space. Consequently, the point spectrum of the Hamiltonian, which is derived from the eigenvalues of this theory, becomes inherently discrete due to the non-trivial topological properties of the configuration space. We examine the cohomology groups of the configuration manifold and demonstrate that its integer-valued first Betti number, describing the number of zero modes in the Hamiltonian, is non-zero. We establish that the discrete nature of the point spectrum of the Hamiltonian is influenced by the topological properties of the configuration space. We propose a new topological classification for quantum systems based on the real wave function formalism, using both the Poincar\'{e} and Seiberg-Witten invariants of the 3-manifold obtained from the metric of the configuration space. We propose a modified version of the metric dimension of graphs, referred to as the $\tau$-trimmed metric dimension, that considers the distances between at least $\tau$ proportion of vertices in a graph. The metric dimension of a graph $G$ with this characteristic is then defined as the minimum size of a subset of vertices that satisfy the aforementioned condition. This concept applies to all graphs, particularly those that are infinite, as the value can be set to either 0 or $\infty$. On the other hand, for finite graphs, the metric dimension is assigned a value of either 0 or the smallest integer that satisfies the given condition. Our objective is to determine the upper limit on the $\tau$-trimmed metric dimension of finite graphs. To accomplish this, we present tight bounds on the metric dimension of specific graphs, particularly those with short shortest paths and those with unique distances. Additionally, we formulate the problem as an NP-hard combinatorial optimization issue and suggest two approximate algorithms. We evaluate these algorithms and the outcomes for various values of $\tau$ in different types of finite graphs. Specifically, we examine infinite graphs and show that the upper limit on the metric dimension is proportional to the logarithm of the graph size for unweighted graphs, as the value of $\tau$ approaches 1. On the other hand, for weighted graphs, as the value of $\tau$ approaches 1/2, the upper limit on the metric dimension is proportional to the square root of the graph size. Ultimately, we present guidelines for identifying the optimal vertices in a finite graph that satisfy the given condition. These guidelines utilize a binary search approach and are dependent on the graph's representation. Additionally, we suggest a different approach that uses graph traversal, as well as an algorithm that efficiently identifies the optimal vertices in a tree. Finally, we examine the time complexity of the problem and compare it to the time complexity of finding a spanning tree in a graph. Specifically, we show that identifying the vertices that satisfy the given condition for a given value of $\tau$ in a tree is a constant factor more complex than finding a spanning tree in the tree. Furthermore, we show that this holds true for various algorithms, as well as different representations of the tree. Lastly, we present an algorithm that efficiently identifies the vertices that satisfy the given condition for a given value of $\tau$ in a particular type of graph. Machine learning algorithms are often applied to make accurate predictions, but our research explores the possibility of modeling that goes beyond accuracy, especially in ethical and social dilemmas where absolute certainty might not be desirable. We propose the concept of Indecision Forests, a machine learning model that learns under quantified uncertainty to represent skeptical argument-based inference. In contrast to traditional machine learning, Indecision Forests use arguments with weightings and qualifications such as 'probably' or 'given to believe', rather than straightforward facts. By representing arguments in this way, Indecision Forests can learn to make nuanced decisions, even in scenarios where there is no consensus. In our study, real-world applications like medical diagnosis and disputes about climate change have shown that skeptical reasoning can lead to better outcomes than the sole use of accuracy, especially when facts are incomplete. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Indecision Forests through experiments in these domains, highlighting their potential to shape decision-making processes and promote more thoughtful reasoning in a variety of fields. At the same time, our model also raises important ethical considerations, including the risk of spreading misinformation and the challenge of balancing accuracy with other values, which deserve to be carefully weighed. In the long run, Indecision Forests could play a significant role in promoting transparency and accountability in high-stakes decision-making contexts. This variant integrates PrunedDTW's strategy with an additional discard option, resulting in enhanced performance.  Both algorithms were tested in a similarity search task and the results show that PrunedDTW outperforms other approaches by a significant margin, while Early Discarding PrunedDTW achieves even better execution times and reduces memory consumption with minimal time complexity.  Experimental evaluations confirm that PrunedDTW and Early Discarding PrunedDTW excel in various settings, demonstrating their superiority over other efficient DTW variants.  Additionally, Early Discarding PrunedDTW offers improved convenience through a simpler implementation.  A comprehensive evaluation of these algorithms was carried out using signal datasets, which included readings from pressure sensors, speech signals, and accelerometer data.  The introduction of Early Discarding PrunedDTW is expected to facilitate efficient similarity searches in a range of real-world applications. This study examines how instruction affects the testing abilities of college students. The researcher tested the hypothesis that instruction focusing on testing, accompanied by relevant feedback, would enhance students' skills in this area. To gather data, the researcher analyzed the responses of 81 students from two university courses. One group received extensive feedback on their work, while another group received conceptual feedback based on questions they were asked to consider. The results showed that conceptual feedback was associated with higher scores on a testing project, while the relationship between feedback and score was not consistent for the thorough feedback group. When considering both instruction and feedback, the researcher found that instruction played a more significant role in determining project scores. The results of this study are limited due to the small sample size and the specific context in which they were gathered. The researcher suggests that testing educators could improve student outcomes by providing more selective feedback in the future. To advance this idea, the researcher offers several potential strategies for refining the feedback process. The researcher also proposes several avenues for further investigation. The data collected for this study are accessible through a public repository. To replicate the results of this study, testers are welcome to contact the researcher. In domains where decisions have significant legal or social repercussions, users of machine learning models demand more transparent explanations for their predictions. While some studies investigate the feasibility of explaining predictions in subtasks, there is a growing need for explanations that cover the entire prediction process. This research develops a novel approach that combines concept analysis and ILP to provide users with understandable justifications for all predictions made by a DNN. Our method is the first to integrate (i) the generation of explanatory rules with (ii) the identification of underlying concepts, resulting in a dual merge of expertise that surpasses existing single-fusion methods. Through empirical evaluation on diverse datasets, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing explanation techniques and successfully translates rule explanations into human-friendly concepts, all within a reasonable time frame. Specifically, our experiment on the Medical Imaging Modality Prediction task shows that our method surpasses state-of-the-art explanation methods by 14% in terms of clarity and 12% in terms of conciseness, while also matching the accuracy of the DNN. Notably, our approach successfully provided visual explanations for predictions made on chest X-ray images, highlighting the importance of underlying concepts like infections or tumors in line with medical expertise. Our findings indicate that merging expertise from different domains can yield exceptional results in providing transparent explanations for DNN predictions. Furthermore, this research lays the groundwork for the development of more interpretable DNNs by pinpointing the crucial role of input features in predicting outcomes. Ultimately, our approach empowers users with insightful explanations that can be easily understood, fostering greater trust in and comprehension of DNN-driven decisions. The accompanying code and datasets are available for reproduction of our results at https://github.com/alexanderhein/Explainability-DNN. Additionally, the generated explanations and concept analyses are available at https://explainability-hein.github.io/. Current state-of-the-art graph convolutional networks (GCNs) exhibit impressive performance on various node-level and graph-level classification tasks, however, they are inherently limited by applying a uniform transformation to neighboring nodes, overlooking specific connections and weights, a problem that exacerbates as networks grow in size. This 'over-blurring' GCN limitation, lacks systematic examination, and existing approaches often resort to stacking multiple GCN layers to compensate, despite this merely shifts the focus to broader spatial areas, rather than improving the model's discriminatory capability. To address this issue, we critically evaluate the effectiveness of GCNs under different architectures, and our surprising discovery shows that simply rearranging the operations of GCN layers can substantially boost performance, outperforming existing solutions. This research provides the first systematic analysis of GCN architectures and uncovers the inherent 'over-blurring' limitation of GCNs, a crucial finding that will enable the development of more accurate machine learning models for graph-structured data in the future. This analysis explores the continuous representation of the Q-shift operator in the context of the fractional power of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on compact, smooth manifolds. Utilizing techniques from fractional calculus and function extension, we define and study the fractional series manipulators (FSMs) associated with the Q-shift operator. Building on existing theories of half-extensions and Fourier series, we establish connections between FSMs and the discrete Hardy spaces on manifolds. Specifically, we identify the primary ideals of the first type of FSMs with the Fourier series projections of the corresponding Hardy spaces. This relationship enables us to derive novel characterizations of the Hardy spaces in terms of FSMs, thereby extending previous findings on the circle and the torus to more general geometric settings. Moreover, our study offers a discrete perspective on the fractional powers of the Laplace-Beltrami operator and the forward and backward Q-shift operators, which may be of independent interest. Finally, as applications of our findings, we establish the equivalence between the first type of FSMs and the first type of q-Fourier series manipulators, where the latter is defined using specific techniques from q-calculus. Additionally, we derive conditions under which the second type of FSMs can be expressed as the product of a first type FSM and a singular function with specific vanishing properties. These results represent novel contributions in the field.

To address this issue, we developed a new task called Neural Painting by Voice, which involves using human-corrected speech recognition inputs to create neural paint representations directly from auditory instructions. Our experiments demonstrate that visual paintings produced from these voice-based inputs are comparable to those generated from written instructions in terms of their semantic authenticity and overall quality. To facilitate the understanding and replication of our system, we was released under an open-source license, featuring a complete implementation of our code and a user-friendly interface for generating neural paintings. Additionally, we conducted a detailed study of the effectiveness of our approach and the sources of variation in the quality of generated images. In contrast to earlier, two-dimensional studies, our model reveals that neutrino instabilities primarily occur near the core's shock wave and are driven by the interaction of neutrinos and non-Uniform matter. Notably, as the star's matter becomes more aligned, the likelihood of neutrino flavor instability decreases. Our results show that the characteristic 'finger' shape of neutrino flavor instabilities is only observable in two-dimensional models and not present in three-dimensional scenarios. We have created an adiabaticity measure that helps predict the likelihood and severity of neutrino flavor instability.
