Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a widely diagnosed neurodevelopmental disorder, and recent studies attempt to identify it through resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI). However, successful identification heavily relies on advanced computational methods. This study aims to contribute to ADHD diagnosis by presenting two essential contributions. Firstly, we develop an unbiased rs-fMRI data analysis method to selectively extract crucial features, which are vital for diagnosing ADHD. Our approach employs a robust strategy to remove non-essential information and uncover the most critical features. Secondly, we employ a state-of-the-art Deep Learning model to demonstrate that our extracted features can effectively diagnose ADHD. Notably, our results showcase that using our approach, models can achieve high diagnostic accuracy, particularly in terms of balanced accuracy, even when training with limited data. Moreover, our findings illustrate the importance of using our proposed features to diagnose ADHD, and that utilizing the entire brain may not be necessary for this purpose. Finally, we examine the correlation between our proposed method's feature selection and the severity of ADHD symptoms, which highlights the potential for our method to provide additional insights beyond simply diagnosing the disorder. Overall, our study demonstrates that our proposed feature selection method and Deep Learning models hold great promise for diagnosing ADHD and understanding the underlying pathology of the disorder. In a discrete-time epidemic SISI model, the number of infective individuals at time t+1 is given by the square of those at time t, minus those that recover, after which they return to being infective. The model assumes a population of N individuals, where the infective population is represented by a variable I_t. The given model is an extension of the previous work by T. Nake on a continuous-time SISI model, as featured in Applied Mathematical Sciences and Computational Tools, 2021. The discrete-time model is particularly relevant in environments where the epidemic period is comparable to or longer than the time unit. The model's equations have been analytically solved for the epidemic curve and the basic reproductive number. The solutions obtained are in line with those of the continuous-time model, as stated in the referenced book. The discrete-time model's outcomes exhibit a perfect replica of the continuous-time model when the time step is extremely small. The critical threshold value of the basic reproductive number, R_0, determines whether the epidemic will subside or spread. The theoretical findings of this discrete-time model have been validated by conducting two simulations, one for each scenario where R_0 is respectively less than or equal to one. The resulting graphs of I_t show an exponential decline when R_0 < 1, whereas the behavior is polynomial when R_0 ≥ 1. The solutions obtained are documented as Theorems 1 and 2. We introduce MadDog, a freely accessible, user-friendly online system for acronym
identification and disambiguation. The tool leverages a comprehensive acronym database
and can be customized using predefined rules or through the submission of tailored
classification algorithms by experts. MadDog supports English and Spanish, with plans
for additional languages. With a simple interface, users can input text and select the
language, then choose from two- to ten-step annotation options. For each step, they can
specify the acronym, its possible meanings, and decide on the relevant interpretation.
This flexible approach allows for expert annotations based on domain-specific knowledge,
or the option to select the most frequent definition from a provided dictionary. Once
configured, MadDog enables real-time annotation of texts, including URLs, and can be
integrated into other platforms via API access. Additionally, annotated texts can be
downloaded in MADIZ format for further use in downstream applications. MadDog aims to
facilitate research and development in acronym identification and disambiguation, while
enabling a wide range of related tasks within natural language processing. To showcase
its capabilities, we have made available several example datasets, covering topics like
biotechnology, medical research, computer science, and diverse domains with domain-specific terminology. These resources can be accessed via our website and used
to compare the performance of different approaches to acronym identification and
disambiguation. To demonstrate the system's efficacy, we have evaluated several recent
methods for acronym identification and disambiguation, including deep learning-based
models, which have achieved high accuracy in various NLP tasks but have not been
previously assessed for their performance on acronym identification. Our analysis
demonstrates that these methods can achieve high precision and recall when identifying and
disambiguate acronyms, and highlights areas for future improvement. MadDog and its
associated resources will be maintained and updated for the next two years. Further details
on the system, as well as the example datasets and evaluation results, can be found on
our website. This research was supported by grant number SEV-2017-B-1051 from the
Conacyt-CONICYT 2017. Additionally, we acknowledge the financial support provided
by the IPN-DIPN grant 003430. We would like to express our gratitude to Dr. Diego María

Early lifelong reinforcement learning research yielded crucial insights into
preserving past experience in subsequent tasks. Nonetheless, the default
evaluation method of comparing cumulative rewards on each individual task
or using a comprehensive aggregate metric like total rewards or time-to-solve
a skill has limitations. These methods fail to capture the transfer of knowledge
from past tasks as effectively as they could. To address this shortcoming, we present
L2Explorer, a framework that facilitates transfer assessment in a range of reinforcement
learning environments. This is accomplished through various task configurations,
including random task selection, interleaved presentation of tasks, and
gradual introduction of more challenging tasks. Our tool also offers a range of
evaluation metrics beyond cumulative rewards and time-to-solve, including success
rates, new skills acquired, project net present value, and the ability to estimate
parameters of interest to lifelong reinforcement learning theorists. Our platform
supports popular reinforcement learning frameworks and can be accessed via a dedicated
website, where users can reproduce our experimental results and explore the L2Explorer
Environment. This environment is now publicly available at https://l2explorer.github.io/.

In medical contexts, extensive data is often generated through various modalities, yet combining these various sources of information to enhance diagnosis is underexplored. To address this, our research focuses on developing novel techniques for integrating multimodal retinal data and evaluating their effectiveness in classifying glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy through comparative studies. Our findings indicate that data fusion methods can significantly improve diagnostic accuracy for glaucoma and DR by 8.8% and 4.9%, respectively, when using three different approaches. Furthermore, our analysis of classification details and model performance reveals the advantages of each method, thereby informing the selection of the most suitable approach for specific clinical applications. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, hospitals have implemented strict capacity controls by only admitting patients in critical need of life-saving services, forcing patients requiring intensive care to wait, often in overcrowded and overstrained ICUs. To develop effective strategies for optimizing ICU space, accurate models predicting COVID-19 transmission and disease severity are crucial. To this end, we propose identifying key image characteristics that differentiate ICU-bound patients from those not needing intensive care, by extracting distinct features from X-ray images of COVID-19 patients. Building on existing research, we develop a multi-task convolutional neural network to jointly identify patient age and ICU admission need based on chest X-ray images, and subsequently extract the underlying features driving these predictions. Notably, our approach generates interpretable representations without requiring additional labels or modules. Through extensive experimentation, we uncovered multiple potential image attributes indicative of ICU admission, and uncovered that lung inflammation and patient age significantly influence this prediction. With these findings, healthcare policymakers can make more informed decisions to optimize ICU space and disease management, while clinicians can gain a deeper understanding of the visual cues and patient demographics influencing ICU admission during the pandemic. Additionally, our model can be adapted for other critical conditions, by leveraging image data and clinical labels to pinpoint key attributes driving disease severity and transmission. With this capability, healthcare systems can prepare for future pandemics by developing data-driven strategies for allocating critical resources during outbreaks. To expand a question-answering system's capabilities, it's beneficial to identify previously unseen answer intents that can be learned from partially labeled data. However, existing approaches have limitations, including requiring a vast amount of unlabeled data and being confined to specific domains. A new proposal, called Next Intent Prediction (NIP), turns this challenge into a ranking task, aiming to identify the next intent given a pair of questions and their respective answers. NIP's advantages include being data-efficient and domain-independent and requires only basic labels. A pre-trained language model and contrastive loss are employed to enhance the ranking process. Experimental results on three datasets demonstrate NIP's superiority over existing methods and its ability to outperform the current state-action model with minimal data. NIP is also shown to have more consistent performance with fewer unlabeled examples. The proposed approach has potential applications in multi-task learning and providing general question answers. The code and dataset are available at a shared repository. NIP's performance is compared to other approaches using three evaluation metrics, including accuracy, loss, and unlabeled data requirements. NIP consistently outperforms or matches the performance of other approaches, such as using a pre-trained transformer with contrastive loss, on intent classification, and a state-action model that uses a pre-trained model on a specific dataset, on two question-answering tasks. NIP is also shown to have a data requirement similar to a fine-tuning approach, but with fewer unlabeled examples. NIP is distinguished from other approaches by having a pre-trained model component and a contrastive loss component. A pre-trained model component improves the ranking by providing general features, while a contrastive loss component refines the ranking by contrasting intent features. The contrastive loss component is shown to have a significant impact on NIP's performance. The original CPN serves as a versatile, feature-rich alternative to existing image representation methods. It can be applied to any downstream task by being refined with a specific goal in mind. Notably, when used for the task of object recognition, it has been shown to be more effective than alternative methods. However, a major drawback of the CPN is that it relies on a predetermined graph structure, which can hinder its performance if the graph is suboptimal. In an effort to address this issue, the graph structure of the CPN can be dynamically adjusted using a neural network. This allows for a more effective distribution of information within the network, which in turn enhances the overall representation of the data. As such, the dynamic graph CPN offers a more flexible and effective solution for data representation. In contrast to the original CPN, the dynamic graph CPN can be viewed as a form of graph neural network (GNN). Nonetheless, it is still distinct from traditional GNNs in that it is an expert network, meaning that it is refined with a specific task in mind. In contrast to traditional GNNs, which are often applied as feature extractors, the dynamic graph CPN can be applied as either a feature extractor or a classifier. Notably, when used as a classifier, it has been shown to be more effective than alternative methods. In particular, when used for the task of semantic segmentation, it has been shown to be more effective than a patch prediction network (PPN) that was developed in a related study. Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) being optimized for efficient use. Recent research has focused on automatically optimizing MCMs for minimal hardware use. Past approaches have either selected one optimal multiplier or used combinations of multipliers to reduce area, but did not consider reconfiguring circuits to reduce area further. This work builds on previous research and introduces a novel method that not only selects the best single multiplier but also explores various circuit configurations using different multipliers to find the optimal overall design. Our approach has been successfully tested on several benchmarks and the results show a significant reduction in area, averaging 24.7% less hardware use compared to existing optimal single-monomial designs, and also demonstrating an additional 13.6% reduction in area compared to designs using multiple monomials. Additionally, our method demonstrates high reconfigurability, with many of the optimal configurations being easily modifiable in response to changes in the constant or multiplier. Our area-optimal design can also be converted into a time-optimal design, showcasing the potential for improved performance in software and hardware designs. Overall, our method provides a versatile solution for MCM optimization. The tool used in this research is available for public use at https://github.com/ahmed-abdelkader/MCM_TCME. The intersection of neural networks and quantum computing holds vast potential for
breakthroughs in multiple disciplines. Despite quantum neural networks' relatively
recent inception, researchers have explored various architectures, proposed
innovative algorithms, and applied them to challenging problems, such as quantum
state learning and phase estimation. This article offers an in-depth review of the
fundamental principles and design choices behind quantum neural networks, a
detailed analysis of prominent applications and the intricate technical difficulties
involved. Additionally, the article outlines future research avenues that could
enable the development of scalable and practical quantum neural networks. One such
approach is the integration of hybrid quantum-classical models, which can leverage
the strengths of both architectures to effectively solve complex problems. By
leveraging quantum computing's unique capabilities, quantum neural networks may
significantly outperform their classical counterparts in specific tasks. However, a
key obstacle to widespread adoption lies in the current limited number of available
quantum processing units (CPUs), which hinders large-scale experimentation. This
article also proposes potential solutions to overcome these hurdles, such as
utilizing simulation-based research and combining quantum and classical computing
methods to develop practical and effective quantum neural networks. By addressing
these challenges and building on recent advancements, researchers can drive the
development of scalable quantum neural networks that unlock new computational
potential. This article serves as a comprehensive guide to the field, offering
insights to researchers and practitioners who wish to contribute to the growth of
quantum neural networks. This article is primarily based on a recent survey paper
arXiv:2101.06725, which has been updated to reflect the latest research developments.

The proposed wave relations are defined by the linearized perturbations of fluid conservation equations, taking into account heat fluxes in the case of dissipative forces. Our findings indicate that the conventional and conservative wave relations are applicable in cases where the dissipation rate is negligible. Moreover, we have established conditions under which the conservative wave relations are uniquely determined. In scenarios where the dissipation rate is non-zero, our results demonstrate that the linearized perturbations of fluid conservation equations lead to two distinct wave relations, which must be satisfied simultaneously. This contrasts with the conventional approach, yielding a single wave relation. Our work has the potential to benefit a broad range of phenomena, including the study of relativistic jets in active galactic nuclei and neutron star mergers. Initially, we consider the quantum mechanical properties of these black holes in a state of thermal equilibrium with the surrounding cosmological environment. Subsequently, we develop a classical description of the radiation within the expanding universe, taking into account both matter-dominated and dark energy-dominated phases. To provide more personalized recommendations to users, session-based recommendation has gained significant attention in recent years. Due to the limited information in each session, incorporating information from other sessions is a valuable approach to enhance the quality of recommendations. Since sessions can be viewed as nodes in a graph, with connections between related sessions, the session-based recommendation task can be treated as a graph-based problem. Building upon this graph representation, we have developed a self-supervised co-training framework for session-based recommendation. This framework utilizes inductive biases to generate pseudo-labels for unsupervised nodes, which are then combined with supervised node labels to enhance the performance of the recommender system. Experimental evaluations have shown that our proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art results on four public datasets, and when compared to existing methods, it demonstrates superior scalability and generalizability. Specifically, our approach has an average improvement of 3.6% in ranking accuracy and 1.3% in click-through rate compared to the best performing baseline models, while requiring significantly fewer parameters (98% reduction). Additionally, our framework exhibits at least 3x faster training times than the baseline methods. A detailed analysis has also shown that our approach can adapt to diverse datasets and even achieve a 9% improvement in ranking accuracy when applied to the TripAdvisor dataset without any fine-tuning. The source code of this project has been made publicly available at https://github.com/Chen-123456/SSGCT. Furthermore, the pre-trained models can be accessed at https://github.com/Chen-123456/SSGCT/tree/master/model_weights. To facilitate further research, we have also released the TripAdvisor dataset at https://github.com/Chen-123456/TripAdvisor. This dataset can be utilized for evaluating the performance of session-based recommendation methods, as well as other related tasks. In summary, our proposed framework has shown exceptional results across multiple evaluation metrics, while also showcasing its adaptability and efficiency. Consequently, it has the potential to significantly enhance the performance of standard session-based recommendation methods. Moreover, our approach has been made fully public, allowing for the reproduction of our results and the exploration of new research avenues. Therefore, this paper can serve as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to improve the state-of-the-art in session-based recommendation. More importantly, our proposed framework has been successfully applied to the TripAdvisor dataset without any fine-tuning, underscoring its versatility and practical value. Consequently, it is likely that our approach will be utilized in numerous real-world applications and products

We examine the problem of developing robust regulators in reinforcement learning, particularly those using probabilistic model-based policy search methods which assume an accurate dynamic model. Traditional robust control techniques aim to minimize the largest possible bounded variation in system outputs. Building on this concept, we generalize the problem and develop a novel approach, finding a regulator that minimizes the largest possible outcome variation under probabilistic model-based policy search, given uncertainty in system dynamics. A probabilistic theoretical guarantee is provided for this approach, demonstrating the relationship between our generalized robust regulator and the optimal solution. Furthermore, we apply this approach to a civil aviation problem, generating efficient and robust regulators for low-altitude approaches. Experimental results show that our method produces robust controllers competitive with optimal control solutions, while outperforming a non-robust alternative in achieving safe system outputs. Additionally, the findings confirm that our approach can alleviate system oscillations and safely land an aircraft in the absence of perfect dynamics information. A Python implementation of the method is included in the provided repository.

To validate the extremality of our constructed linear programming system in the context of the Turan problem, we also developed an alternative formulation centered around the exponents of even, homogeneous, zero-degree, multivariable polynomials. Notably, the outcome of our investigation corresponds with the known extremal values of the standard (0-1) $\ell_2$-norm of the same combinatorial problem, a value that had been the subject of the 16th Hungarian Mathematical Competition's problem for over five decades. Our method of analysis also enables us to derive an exact count of the number of extremal graphs for the $\ell_2$-norm under consideration. To achieve this, we developed an algorithm centered around the geometric interpretation of the extremal values of the linear programming formulation that had been set up in our study. As a result, the exact number of extremal graphs can be calculated exactly for all sufficiently large $n$. This paper introduces a novel multi-class weather identification dataset with a hierarchical structure, comprising three levels of classification. The primary classification encompasses nine distinct weather types, while sub-categories offer more precise classifications for certain weather conditions. To enhance the diversity of the weather categorization task, a binary image transformation technique - horizontal image mirroring - is applied to the training set. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a series of evaluations, which compare the performance of various Convolutional Neural Network architectures under different training configurations. The study conducts a thorough assessment of traditional evaluation metrics, alongside two alternative measures - top-n accuracy and sensitivity of the classification. The top-performing network, referred to as Wide ConvNet2, achieves an impressive accuracy rate of 64% across the primary weather categories and surpasses alternative architectures in accuracy and top-1 accuracy together with other methods, especially when faced with augmented training data. The integration of horizontal image mirroring in the training process contributes to a 6% improvement in the average accuracy of the networks evaluated. The research findings, along with the newly developed dataset and associated evaluation methods, are intended to contribute to and advance the field of weather-based image classification. The results of both simulated and real-world tests demonstrate that the model can be relied upon to control the gripper in a challenging task, such as picking and placing small objects. Moreover, the model can be updated during physical testing, showcasing its value in applications where adaptability is crucial. The development of this approach could pave the way for a range of applications, including automated grasping in diverse environments. One of the fundamental techniques in optimization, gradient descent, has seen its share of complications when dealing with non-euclidean data, particularly with nonconvex objectives and complex structures like tensor norms. Our proposed method, the Organic Gradient Descent (OGD), resolves this issue by providing a straightforward algorithm that converges globally. By incorporating the Nesterov acceleration in a simplified manner, OGD achieves improved convergence rates. Our analysis covers three key settings: sparse nonconvex optimization, where a limited number of parameters can be adjusted, and two scenarios with explicit constraints. Our results demonstrate that OGD surpasses the performance of existing methods, such as Block Coordinate Ascent and Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent, in all test cases. Furthermore, our findings include convergence speed estimates and a theoretical guarantee of local convergence. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexandruMunteanu/OrganicGradientDescent. Our research demonstrates that optimization can be both elegant and simple, and we hope to inspire a renewed appreciation for this field. Our analysis covers applications such as sparse additive models, tensor regression, and our results even extend to other recently-proposed organic methods like the SemiStochastic Gradient Descent, demonstrating better performance and faster convergence rates. Our final example showcases how OGD can be effectively applied to deep learning models using automatic differentiation, significantly reducing training times by up to 20x. Our work culminates in a public Python package, organic-grad, that includes a comprehensive collection of optimized sparse models and a clear, simple API for easy integration into popular optimization frameworks. Our research aims to promote the organic gradient descent as a versatile, efficient, and efficient optimization technique that can be broadly applied. A machine-learning-based approach is introduced to derive the power spectrum of a signal from a single observation of a spectrum. This technique is applied to the absorption spectra of quasars to improve the reconstruction of the density power spectrum of the intergalactic medium (IGM). The method utilizes a convolutional neural network trained on simulated data comprising various types of observation noise and a broad range of redshifts. When tested against simulated data, the network's performance is found to approximately reproduce the underlying power spectrum at a fraction of the original measurement error. Additionally, we identify certain mathematical structures that are naturally associated with these projections, proving that these structures are unique and independent. We further prove that these results are not merely theoretical, but also have practical implications in the form of functional equations for the specific mathematical structures. Finally, we investigate how these results are affected when the algebra is modified to only include differential operators of an arbitrary positive degree. Crucially, the key findings of this research are independent of the choice of basis or ordering. We hope that these outcomes will contribute to the development of novel methods in the field of mathematical structure theory. To effectively interact with customers, customer service representatives must possess specialized knowledge. We have developed a digital assistant that can be adapted to various roles such as customer support, entertainment, etc., and is capable of engaging in natural conversations while requiring minimal domain-specific expertise. Our approach relies on the underlying knowledge base of large language models, allowing us to focus on the subject matter and not the specific terminology. We present two primary methods for our digital assistant: a role-based language model handler and a role-specific language model handler. The former handles conversations with multiple role-based models, while the latter is tailored to a particular role. Our tests demonstrate that our open-domain dialogue system is capable of withstanding a range of topics and role changes. We compare the performance of our digital assistant to that of a zero-shot language model and find that our approach yields better results in various roles. Additionally, our open-domain dialogue system outperforms a zero-shot language model and a dialogue model trained on customer conversations. We make our code and role specifications available for public use. We aim to expand our digital assistant to encompass a broader range of roles and applications in the future. We believe our digital assistant can be applied to numerous settings beyond customer support, such as social media platforms, where a role-specific open-domain dialogue system could enhance user experiences by providing relevant and engaging responses. We propose an upgraded RingCT protocol that integrates a new delegation feature, allowing users to transfer coins owned by another individual while maintaining anonymity. To accomplish this, our scheme leverages an extended public key infrastructure, where a user obtains a certificate comprising two components: an identifiable public key and an unidentifiable partial public key. When transacting anonymously, the user publicly signs the partial public key, then uses it in conjunction with the identifiable public key to sign the transaction, thereby verifying ownership. To enhance security, our model involves a pairing-based delegation framework that is non-frameable and resistant to several types of attacks, such as identity theft and counterfeit transactions. In-context learning allows for efficient and economical knowledge acquisition, and can be improved by utilizing models pre-trained on diverse datasets. However, the impact of varying training corpora on this learning approach has not been extensively investigated. In this study, we examine how models pre-trained on different data sets respond to in-context learning, specifically looking at how they perform when prompted with questions drawn from those same data sets, or with questions that are more alien to the training corpus. Our primary objective is to investigate the impact of ground sound on aerial vehicle navigation. Ground sound is a type of acoustic signal that emerges from the interaction between the vehicle's propellers and the ground, leading to the generation of infrasonic and sub-bass frequencies. These low-frequency vibrations pose a significant challenge to vehicle stability, particularly in aerial navigation. To address this issue, we propose the concept of ground sound propagation models, which enable the calculation of ground sound intensity at a specified distance from the vehicle. Our research demonstrates the existence of two ground sound regimes: a quiet regime characterized by a linear relationship and a loud regime marked by a power-law exponent of 6. Our findings are verified through both theoretical analysis and experimental validation. Additionally, we provide a quantitative measure of ground disturbance and suggest an effective approach to mitigate the effect of ground sound. Our investigation contributes to a deeper understanding of the relationship between ground sound and vehicle movement, ultimately paving the way for the development of more robust aerial navigation systems. These systems can effectively navigate through dense environments, such as forests, without being compromised by the ground sound. This study examines three mathematical representations of Leibnizian calculus, 
namely the $\epsilon$-$\delta$, deal I, and real valve frameworks. 
We assess the validity of three key tenets of Leibniz's view on continuous change: 
the vanishing thesis, the threshold thesis, and the coexistence thesis. 
Within the $\epsilon$-$\delta$ framework, the first two theses hold, 
but the third does not. In the deal I framework, 
the first two theses are viable, while the third thesis requires further discussion. 
Within the real valve framework, 
both the vanishing and threshold theses are upheld, rendering the third thesis redundant. 
Our analysis suggests that the deal I framework presents a more accurate depiction of Leibniz's views on change and that it offers a more robust defense against the argument that Leibniz was incoherent. 
Conversely, the real valve framework presents a more conservative defense, 
while the $\epsilon$-$\delta$ framework yields incoherence unless one accepts significant modifications to Leibniz's views. 
Ultimately, the study advocates for a more nuanced understanding of Leibniz's views on change and the nature of infinitesimal calculus. 
Additionally, it highlights an analogy between the deal I and real valve approaches and 
the a priori and a posteriori methods in Kant's metaphysics, 
thus providing a new perspective on this distinction. 
Lastly, the study examines the potential implications of these results on the broader landscape of philosophical research in the history of mathematics. 
In particular, it considers the relevance of these results to four influential studies on the history and philosophy of mathematics, namely Reichenbach's study on the development of Cantor's set theory, 
Quine's study on the nature of reference, 
Kant's Critique of Pure Reason, and Reichenbach's study on the nature of space and time.

By doing so, each module can focus on its local strengths and be less concerned about the others, allowing for more flexible decision-making. Through our design, each module can now independently adjust its gradient based on the relative importance of different parameters, effectively making the training more adaptable. To test the effectiveness of this innovation, we conducted a series of experiments involving the training of convolutional neural networks on various image classification datasets, using different network configurations and hardware setups. The results showed a noticeable improvement in training efficiency and a significant reduction in training time, with the involvement of the regional critic layer. Notably, the best-performing models were often obtained through a careful balance of the number of modules and dataset complexity, with a particular sweet spot observed for the CIFAR-10 dataset. While the involvement of the regional critic layer did improve the overall performance, it did not entirely eliminate the impact of synchronization requirements. NBcoded stands out from traditional approaches by minimizing the need for detailed traffic data and the device's processing power. Our approach involves reengineering the network traffic, breaking it down into binary code sequences that are then classified using a Naive Bayes classifier. This classification method is both accurate and efficient, requiring only a single training example to achieve a high level of performance (97.2% precision, 96.3% recall, and 96.7% accuracy). Our simulation-based evaluation of NBcoded demonstrates exceptional accuracy in identifying various network attacks, along with a significant reduction in false positives and training data requirements. Our proposed solution outperforms current attack detection systems, showcasing the potential to transform existing resource-limited devices into powerful security platforms. Our research builds on recent findings by Tyomkyn, who discovered a growth rate for the number of automorphisms with a specific cyclic order in certain solvable groups. We're able to pinpoint a lower limit for this growth rate and establish that it's asymptotically achievable as the order of the group grows larger. This lower limit is determined by the lengths of the solvable Lie algebras associated with the solvable representations of Sylow subgroups. Notably, our result holds significance due to an unexpected connection with Euler's totient function. This growth rate gives rise to a characteristically simple family of solvable groups, and we leverage this insight to develop a strategy for identifying automorphisms with specific cyclic orders in these groups, thereby contributing to a long-standing open question in group theory. As a byproduct of our work, we gather various group-theoretic findings that might be of individual interest. Lastly, our research also yields an inequality involving the lengths of the solvable Lie algebras associated with fundamental representations of Sylow subgroups. This inequality suggests the possibility of an upper bound on the growth rate, and we verify it for a wide array of solvable groups, but surprisingly, it fails for some groups within specific classes. Consequently, the problem of determining the exact growth rate becomes a complex task dependent on the specific structure of the group. We tackle this challenge for nilpotent groups with a specific abelian structure and derive a closed formula for the number of automorphisms with a specific cyclic order in these groups. We also explore some open questions and conjectures stemming from our work and existing research. Ultimately, our findings provide significant insights into the intricate relationships within the collections of automorphisms of solvable groups. Additionally, our research generates numerous questions and conjectures, and a significant portion of the paper is devoted to addressing them. This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the possibility of observing heavy, heavy, charged and long-lived particles in 13 TeV $pp$ collisions. The search specifically targets particles that interact with matter in a manner similar to the chargino, a supersymmetric particle, and complements previous ATLAS studies. The dataset analyzed consists of the complete data collected during Run 2, which amounts to 139 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity. The search focuses on particles that leave behind distinct tracks and are characterized by reduced energy loss in the pixel detectors, often resulting in the removal of these particles from final particle counts. Two search categories are defined based on the nature of the particles' decays: either as a single particle or as a result of the decay of a $R$-pair. The study considers various signatures, including an isolated track, a track accompanied by high-energy energy loss, distinct tracks and an overall count of tracks with reduced energy loss. The data is analyzed against a range of theoretical backgrounds, and the resulting data is compared to a range of theoretical models, which include the production of long-lived charginos and $R$-pair neutralinos. In the case where the mass of the chargino is less than 1 TeV, several models are consistent with the observed data, while models that predict the production of charged Higgsinos are generally excluded across their entire mass range. On the other hand, models that predict the production of gluinos are generally excluded based on a separate study that focuses on the decay of these particles into various signatures. One specific model of tri-linear Higgs mediation is found to be consistent with the observed data, and the associated charged Higgsino mass range is found to be between 0.4 and 1.1 TeV. In addition, a wide range of other theoretical models are found to be consistently excluded across their entire mass range. Furthermore, models that predict the production of $R$-pair neutralinos are generally excluded based on a separate study that focuses on the decay of these particles into various signatures. One specific model of tri-linear Higgs mediation is found to be consistently excluded across its entire mass range. In summary, this study provides the most comprehensive search for the production of heavy, long-lived, charged particles in the ATLAS dataset, and the results are found to be generally in agreement with the Standard Model of particle physics, while also excluding or confirming a wide range of theoretical models based on supersymmetry

A new concept has emerged in two-dimensional materials called valleytronics that utilizes valley information to enhance the efficiency of devices beyond what's achievable with traditional silicon technology. Valley information can be activated by an external stimulus such as an electric field, and it has been observed that it can interact with the motion of atoms within the material, a process known as electron-phonon coupling. Influencing the valley state by exposing the material to light is a difficult task due to the need for high light intensity and short pulse durations, making it an expensive and logistically challenging process. Recent research has explored alternative methods for activating the valley state without requiring intense light, such as mechanical stress and the use of highly efficient valley-mechanical coupling mechanisms. We have successfully emulated a fermionic system on a quantum circuit simulator by leveraging the analog-digital hybrid method, which utilizes the Meron-Susskind lightcone algorithm as the digital component. This approach not only minimizes qubit utilization but also significantly decreases the size of the computational circuit. Our findings indicate that the analog-digital method can serve as an effective substitute for traditional digital quantum computing in the study of connected fermionic systems. Moreover, we observed that the hybrid method is particularly adaptable for systems with sparse interactions, where it can offer substantial advantages in terms of circuit scale and qubit count. However, for systems featuring extensive interactions, the required analog circuit size increases exponentially, which may render the method less feasible. Nonetheless, even in such cases, the hybrid method can still provide scale and qubit advantages. Ultimately, we believe that the analog-digital hybrid approach has the potential to be a valuable tool in quantum chemistry research. Additionally, we have made the corresponding source code publicly available on the Quantum Open-Source Software website. A key challenge in machine learning lies in balancing a model's accuracy and ability to perform well in unfamiliar situations. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring ways to measure a model's predicted confidence and its capacity for generalization. In this context, a new approach is presented that enables the detection of fake reviews on Amazon by analyzing characteristics extracted from review texts. These features are constructed using a variety of word overlap methods to compare the similarities and differences between adjacent reviews. By employing the Wealth-Index, a new metric that takes into account both these aspects, models can be optimized for either their overall performance or their ability to perform well in new situations. Experimental findings demonstrate that models trained with this new feature tend to perform better at tasks requiring generalization and can be easily adapted for applications like sentiment analysis and product category identification. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits improved performance over existing methods that rely on word-based overlap, such as review topic analysis and word similarity. By leveraging the Wealth-Index, researchers can develop more effective strategies to address the optimization-generalization paradox in natural language processing. Furthermore, the proposed approach can be applied to other tasks and domains to enhance models' generalization capabilities. Vector space embeddings, which encode semantic characteristics of words, can also be utilized to construct features for the Wealth-Index. However, the method presented here does not require such embeddings and can be applied even when they are not available. To validate the efficacy of the proposed approach, the researchers also presented a new metric called the Generalization Wealth-Index (GWI). The GWI measures a model's ability to perform well in new situations by analyzing its performance on reviews that are one to three categories away from its original training data. By employing the GWI, researchers can identify the optimal hyperparameters that maximize a model's generalization capabilities. Moreover, the Wealth-Index and GWI can be applied to construct new features for various natural language tasks. For example, the researchers demonstrated that the Wealth-Index and GWI can be used to build a natural kernel for sentiment analysis. Additionally, the Wealth-Index was employed to create a new dataset for sentiment analysis by analyzing Amazon reviews that are one category apart in terms of the sentiment label. The dataset, called the Wealth-Dataset, exhibits several desirable properties, including a more linear progression in the sentiment labels and a more consistent sentiment across adjacent reviews. Meta-analyses that consider multiple dependent variables beyond just means can be restricted by the limitations of available pool-to-pool covariance estimators. In order to overcome this issue, we've developed new cluster-robust estimators for meta-analyses that take into account the effects of within-study dependencies on both response variables. We've shown that these estimators are consistent, allowing us to extend the classical meta-analytic model to include the shared-proportional-responsiveness meta-analysis, which accounts for dependencies between response variables. We've implemented these new estimators in a package called the metaCRB package for the R language, enabling users to access additional functionality via the metaCRB GUI. We illustrate the utility of our approach with a meta-analysis that combines data from twenty studies examining the relationship between inflammatory markers and cancer risk. We've compared our proposed estimators with existing ones, revealing a significant improvement in their efficiency and a better capacity to resist the influence of within-study dependencies. As a result, our meta-analytic model demonstrates enhanced statistical power, particularly in cases where within-study dependencies are present. Finally, we've highlighted the significance of considering within-study dependencies in a real-world context by re-running the meta-analysis while controlling for correlations between response variables, which shows that neglecting these correlations may lead to biased estimates and incorrect confidence intervals for our primary results. In contrast, we found that using the proposed cluster-robust estimators in conjunction with a Guérin-Suresh model yielded more accurate results and narrower CI widths when correlations between response variables are present. Conversely, we observed that using the Guérin-Suresh model without accounting for within-study dependencies led to broader CI widths and less precise estimates when such correlations do not exist. Consequently, we advocate for the use of cluster-robust estimators in bivariate meta-analyses, particularly when within-study dependencies are present, as evidenced by our results and the implementation of these estimators in the metaCRB package. This study develops a novel integration method to simulate multiple collisions between particles in a contact interaction using a soft-body model. The method assembles a collision kernel from a particle's velocity and position information, then uses this kernel to determine if a collision is imminent based on the particle's trajectory. If a collision occurs within the integration time step, the particles are resolved using a soft-body model; otherwise, a standard collision model is employed. This method is particularly suitable for particle-resolved simulations in complex flows. A key advantage is that it allows for larger integration time steps, reducing computational costs without sacrificing accuracy. This category satisfies the requirements for a continuous category as defined in [Angiuli, Guild, and Tessier 2019], and thus provides a suitable framework for studying continuous logic.  In particular, we examine the properties of $\mathcal{Str}_{\cont}$'s subcategory consisting of complete models, denoted $\mathcal{Str}^{\comp}_{\cont}$, and show it is a complete category in its own right.  This allows us to examine the relationship between types and morphisms in a more abstract algebraic context.  As an alternative, we also introduce the category $\mathcal{Type}_{\cont}$ whose objects are types and whose morphisms are corresponding correspondences as defined in [Tressler 2018], and show that the relationship between types and morphisms can be described by a functor from $\mathcal{Type}_{\cont}$ to $\mathcal{Str}_{\cont}$.  This provides a more general description of the relationship between types and morphisms, and has several applications including a characterization of the types that are maximal, as well as a description of the types that are equivalent to the types of complete models.  Finally, we propose a category whose objects are types, and whose morphisms are corresponding correspondences, and show that the relationship between types is anti-symmetric.  This provides a description of the partial order on the collection of types, and has several applications including a description of the smallest and greatest types that contain a given type, as well as a description of the types that are intermediate between two given types.  This partially ordered category has a number of additional useful properties including that it is a poset-complete category, and that the collection of types is a closed collection in the sense that the types of substructures of any model are all members of the collection. Our investigation focuses on the properties of a Lewis-Benedict-Collins-Kimball state (LCCK) composed of two coupled bosonic modes, one of which undergoes compression while the other remains unaltered. The LCCK state is known for containing a wide range of quantum fluctuations. To understand the impact of classical driving forces on this phenomenon, we examine the Fock space's structure and associated fluctuations as one of the modes is either compressed or expanded. The LCCK state still occupies the heart of the Fock space for any applied force, and the distribution of remaining photons across adjacent Fock states follows a symmetric pattern. I propose an explanation for the fundamental forces' distinctiveness, arguing that gravity's relatively weak force is an inherent result of it being the only force measured retro-causally from the inflationary period. When applied to the quantum realm, this theory demands the application of a time-reversal operator, leading to a complex representation of the Hamiltonian and thus the energy-momentum tensor. This analysis suggests the existence of a macro-quantum coherent state at the onset of the Higgs-Goldstone arena, which corresponds to the present-day universe, and implies the presence of an entropic force acting between small-scale objects. Ultimately, this theory may provide the link between quantum and relativistic theories. 

Furthermore, I discuss several key points, including the absence of a causal relationship between the Higgs-Goldstone and the electromagnetic field, the possibility of a quantum time crisis, the potential for a quantum-based explanation of the universe's flatness, and the feasibility of creating closed and negatively curved universes. Additionally, I outline a possible experiment to detect the entropic force and the retro-causal measurement of gravity. Lastly, I present a fundamental equation that can be used to calculate the universe's energy density from the inflationary period to the present day. 

In the end, I acknowledge that this is an unconventional and speculative theory, but I also emphasize that it is highly consistent with the existing data. Therefore, I urge the scientific community to conduct thorough tests to verify the various predictions made by this model. If validated, this theory may provide a unified understanding of the fundamental forces and the universe's evolution. Conversely, if it fails these tests, it may serve as a valuable precursor to more refined theories, ultimately contributing to the advancement of theoretical physics. 

In the appendices, I have included a detailed derivation of the retro-causal measurement of gravity, the entropic force, and the time-reversal operator, utilizing only the principles of quantum mechanics and general relativity. I have also presented an alternative formulation of the universe's energy-momentum tensor and the Hamiltonian, as well as the potential for a quantum-based explanation of the universe's flatness. Additionally, I have outlined a possible cosmological scenario, where the universe's curvature and matter density are entirely determined by the retro-causal measurement of gravity, the entropic force, and the present-day vacuum Higgs-Goldstone arena. Lastly, I have included a brief discussion on the potential for a quantum-based understanding of black holes and the information paradox.

Several local authorities are seeking efficient methods to regularly assess the condition of their roads, but current techniques are often labor-intensive and expensive.
Research into this area has grown, with most studies focusing on specific regions and using country-specific data and models.
Our project aimed to develop a universal approach that could be applied to various countries with minimal adaptation.
By leveraging advanced neural networks and transfer learning, we can quickly adapt our method to new roads using only a few labeled images.
Our study compares different approaches and transfer learning techniques, then evaluates them using road images from the UK, Germany, and Australia.
The results indicate that a Fine-tuning strategy enabled by a shared pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network produces the best outcomes.
Furthermore, we analyzed how different road types and damage types interact and proposed a new evaluation metric that balances accuracy and fairness. 
Our code and pre-trained models are available on GitHub for other researchers to build upon. 
Our approach has the potential to be used by multiple countries to quickly assess the condition of their roads without having to start from scratch. 
Our method can also be adapted to various environments and enhanced by incorporating other factors that may affect road condition assessment. 
In terms of fairness, our results indicate that a combination of CNN layers can help to identify different road types, and our proposed metric allows for a balance between accuracy and fairness. 
Lastly, we acknowledge the limitations of our study, primarily due to the absence of publicly accessible data for comparison, and we recommend that local authorities consider collecting and sharing their own data for this purpose. 
We also suggest that future research could involve the application of domain adaptation techniques to reduce the need for labeled data and the incorporation of other relevant factors that may affect road condition assessment. 
In summary, our main contributions are the development of a universal approach to road condition assessment and the application of transfer learning and Fine-tuning to this task. 
Additionally, we compared different approaches and evaluated the performance of several CNN models, as well as proposed a new evaluation metric that balances accuracy and fairness. 
Lastly, we highlighted some potential limitations and suggested some potential future research directions. 
In conclusion, we hope that our research will contribute positively to the field and inspire further research. 
We made our code and pre-trained models available on GitHub for other researchers to build upon.

This study examines how a court-mandated mental health program affects those convicted of a crime, specifically whether it leads to improved mental health outcomes and reduced recidivism rates. Using a unique dataset that includes information on treatment completion, I found that requiring therapy has a positive impact on both measures. More specifically, those who complete their treatment experience enhanced mental health benefits and a lower likelihood of future convictions. To determine the program's effect, I employed a combination of statistical analysis, including propensity score methods and a novel technique that accounts for treatment duration. Notably, results indicate that the benefits of the program are greatest for individuals who might have otherwise not sought mental health services. Additionally, I found that the program's effect varies depending on the severity of the offender's mental health at the time of their conviction. Specifically, those with more severe mental health needs experience greater improvements in mental health outcomes following treatment. This research highlights the potential of mental health treatment to drive positive outcomes for both mental health and criminal justice systems. This work outlines a method to identify anomalies in continuous data streams by analyzing trends using Hidden Markov Models. These models represent a specific pattern in the data, and compare actual readings to the expected pattern to determine likelihood. Our anomaly detection method uses a modified version of this analysis, adapting it for use with multiple gauge datasets. Each gauge produces separate likelihood results, which are combined to create an overall anomaly score. This score indicates the degree to which a reading deviates from the expected pattern, and can be set to trigger specific actions. To effectively manage false positive rates, our method utilizes a dynamic threshold technique, adjusting the anomaly score threshold based on the trade-off between accuracy and sensitivity. This approach is particularly suitable for use cases where some degree of error is acceptable, and demonstrates its efficacy through applications in airline delay forecasting and traffic estimation. Further details on these cases, as well as the implementation of our method, are provided in the accompanying paper. The source code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/whitewaterkul/hmm_anomaly under the term MIT License. Additionally, a cloud-based environment containing all required packages can be found at https://kuldip-whitewater.github.io/hmm_anomaly/. Our method is designed to be model-agnostic, and can be applied to a variety of datasets across different domains by adjusting the gauge likelihood analysis. This flexibility is illustrated through an example case involving stock market analysis. To facilitate easy integration of our method into existing projects, we have created a Python package named 'hmm_anomaly' that can be installed via pip. This package includes a range of features, such as gauge likelihood analysis, dynamic threshold calculation, and anomaly scoring, among others. By providing a comprehensive set of tools, our package enables users to develop and train their own anomaly detection models. These models can then be used to identify anomalies in various datasets, and even integrate with existing classification models to improve performance. Our method is compatible with a variety of datasets, and can be adapted for use with streaming data by utilizing techniques such as windowing and buffering. Achieving complete data protection under standard differential privacy comes with significant costs, hence a modified approach, one-sided differential privacy, is implemented to minimize expenses. However, the standard evaluation method for one-sided differential privacy focuses solely on relative gains or losses, which may lead to underestimating the exposure of sensitive information when attributes depend on each other.

For instance, suppose we have a database containing a student's GPA and their parents' income, the release of their GPA inevitably reveals their parents' income. The problem arises when we evaluate the exposure of the income after a transformation that increases the GPA by a relative unit, as the income's exposure is not relative to the GPA but rather to other factors. The research mentioned in the problem does not account for such situations where attributes are interconnected, which can result in a misleading assessment of the data's one-sided differential privacy. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a more comprehensive framework that measures the data's one-sided differential privacy while considering the interdependence of attributes. The framework enables us to derive a more accurate evaluation method for releasing dependent attributes, as well as to uncover previously unacknowledged vulnerabilities, which we term attribute exposure risks. The evaluation method consists of two techniques: attribute influence and attribute coverage, which respectively assess how much an attribute is influenced by other attributes and how much coverage an attribute provides to other attributes. The techniques are further demonstrated through three real-world applications: (1) the exposure of individuals' identities when releasing social media information, (2) the exposure of students' family information when releasing demographic data, and (3) the exposure of medical condition information when releasing related attributes. The research also introduces three methods to mitigate attribute exposure risks, including attribute removal, parameter adjustment, and weighted averaging. The outcome of our study shows that attribute coverage risk is always equal to 1, whereas attribute influence risk can be minimized through the removal of attributes with the lowest influence values. The research also reveals that when adjusting parameters, smaller attributes tend to have a greater impact than larger ones, as evidenced by experiments using Gaussian mechanisms and the Frank-Wolfe algorithm, as well as a empirical analysis of Amazon Mechanical Turk. Lastly, the application of the simple weighted averaging method to the empirical data shows that attribute influence and attribute coverage can be effectively reduced by assigning lower weights to smaller attributes and higher weights to larger attributes. Improving the accuracy of hyperspectral imaging is a critical goal in various fields, and enhancing image quality by supplanting or correcting faulty bands has been the focus of previous studies. These studies assume that (1) each band can be corrupted, (2) a complete and accurate guide to damaged bands is available, and (3) the corruption of bands is unlinked. In realistic scenarios however, multiple bands may be affected (as in the case of lens damage), and such factorisation can lead to inaccurate results. To address these issues, we introduce a new task called guided hypergraph reconstruction (GHR), which aims to improve the quality of hyperspectral images by replacing or correcting faulty bands, with the assistance of a partial guide to damaged bands, and where band corruption is interconnected. We then propose an innovative GHR approach, where we first construct a hypergraph from the input image and utilise partial guidance to generate initial node and edge weights. We then iteratively optimise the weights of nodes and edges to produce the best possible reconstruction, with the support of the partial guide. Our approach, which we call guided hypergraph reconstruction (GHR), is tested on various corrupted hyperspectral images and outperforms existing band-wise reconstruction methods by up to 4.4% in terms of the CIEDE2000 colour metric. Our framework is also compatible with existing unguided HR methods and can further boost their performance by up to 3.2%. Our code is available online at https://github.com/zhengzheng0626/GHR. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach, which we call Guided Hypergraph Reconstruction (GHR), delivers superior image quality, with a significant improvement in index r. Moreover, our framework is compatible with existing HR methods and can further enhance the quality of hyperspectral images. Our framework is versatile and can be applied to various real-world scenarios, as evidenced by the examples provided in the paper. To quantify this manipulation, we'll focus on a method involving the application of the Frankford metric to assess the fairness of a district map. This metric considers the number of winning candidates in each district. By applying techniques from simulated cooling, such as the Monte Carlo method and simulated annealing, we'll find the minimum temperature that results in a map that favors one party. Case studies using data from North Carolina will examine the effectiveness of this method. Additionally, we'll explore an alternative method involving the application of the Wasserstein metric to assess district population deviations. Our work will be based on a publicly available Python package for evaluating voting district maps. To facilitate reproducibility, our code and associated data will be shared on the GitHub platform. This research proposes an innovative method for defect identification in patterned fabric images. The proposed technique leverages Gabor features harvested from Hierarchical Oriented Gradient (GHOG) descriptors to enhance descriptor representation and, in turn, improves the accuracy of low-rank decomposition-based fabric defect detection. By integrating GHOG with the conventional Gabor features, our results demonstrate a substantial boost in performance, with the newly developed descriptor framework and associated matrix decomposition technique yielding a Turkmenistan fabric defect detection accuracy rate of 97.75%, an 8.57% improvement over the existing techniques. Furthermore, our approach is evaluated on a diverse range of fabric types, showcasing its effectiveness and demonstrating a significant advancement in fabric defect identification. Additionally, our study highlights the supremacy of the proposed GHOG framework over alternative methods such as SIFT, SURF, and Gabor features. Notably, our technique achieves superior performance with reduced computational complexity, thereby facilitating its deployment in real-time fabric defect detection applications. A comprehensive evaluation against state-of-the-art techniques is presented, with our method outperforming or surpassing existing approaches in all tested scenarios. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games is their slow pace, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of how they process input and generate output.
Our text game environment, TextWorldExpress, has been optimized to increase performance, allowing for a million actions per second.
TextWorldExpress achieves this improved speed by using a more efficient game API and allowing for the use of modern multi-core CPUs and high-performance networks. 
Our results show that while the new environment poses technical difficulties, it also presents opportunities for enhancing agent performance, with the fastest agents demonstrating a notable performance boost. 
To facilitate widespread adoption, we're open-sourcing TextWorldExpress and inviting the community to take part in a collaborative effort to develop the first open-source challenge based on this platform. 
Our goal is to promote fair, standardized evaluations that can help agents achieve optimal results and showcase their capabilities. 
The resources for getting started can be found at our project website: https://textworld.github.io/te/. 
Feel free to reach out to us with any questions or suggestions: [email: textworld@gmail.com](mailto:textworld@gmail.com). 
We're looking forward to collaborating with the community!

TextWorldExpress is based on TextWorld, which you can find at: https://textworld.github.io/.

The rapid spread of misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines necessitates swift countermeasures. Social media platforms like Twitter, where such misinformation spreads, can also be leveraged to track this issue. However, detecting and differentiating varying forms of misinformation (i.e., false information that is partially or entirely incorrect) on this platform is complex. In contrast, identifying accepted misinformation (i.e., widely believed false information) is relatively straightforward by focusing on retweets. A proposed framework, consisting of natural language processing and machine learning techniques, aims to distinguish accepted from rejected misinformation by analyzing unique characteristics. These include the source of the information, discourse on Twitter, and user perspectives, as well as the geographic distribution of users. The proposed system also incorporates an innovative network approach to gather relevant information, such as the number of Twitter users, retweets, and likes. Preliminary evaluations using a small dataset indicate that the proposed framework has potential, with areas for further improvement and potential applications. The developed approach can be applied to various other domains beyond COVID-19 vaccine misinformation to analyze and understand the dynamics of misinformation. Producing attosecond pulses (ASPs) via high-order harmonic generation (HHG) in noble gases has become a major focus. To increase the efficiency and control of ASP generation, researchers have employed various external influences, such as magnetic fields and spatially modulated lasers. This study demonstrates that a controlled, very strong transverse electric field can optimize ASP production by affecting the HHG process in nonlinear systems. By applying a 3D Monte Carlo simulation, we analyzed the effects of the laser and ionization fields on the temporal and spectral characteristics of the ASPs. Our findings reveal that a certain field strength can optimize ASP production by reducing its duration and increasing its power, ultimately resulting in a higher electron recollision probability and hence a greater high-energy cut-off (HEC) in the HHG spectrum. This research offers a novel approach for regulating ASP generation and increasing the HEC, which is crucial for producing higher-energy ASPs and achieving better spatial and temporal control. Additionally, this concept has the potential to be applied not only to nonlinear phenomena but also to the manipulation of electronic dynamics in atoms and molecules. Furthermore, this research may provide insights into the electronic structure of molecules through the manipulation of their electronic dynamics using external fields. Finally, this study provides a framework for the experimental implementation of our findings, which could enable the production of shorter, more powerful ASPs and provide valuable insights into the behavior of atoms and molecules under strong external fields. Ultimately, this could lead to groundbreaking breakthroughs in our understanding of their electronic structure and the manipulation of electronic dynamics. Additionally, our research has the potential to be applied to various fields such as radiation sources, medical imaging, and the manipulation of matter. Lastly, we acknowledge that this research could have far-reaching implications for various applications, including the manipulation of matter.

The success of Deep Learning methods in image recognition tasks has driven the development of analogous techniques for 3D data, such as point cloud classification and semantic segmentation tasks. Despite the potential of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), several challenges such as efficient spatial reasoning, graph construction, and batch normalization have hindered their practical application. This study addresses these challenges by introducing a novel GCN architecture, GCN-Swish, which incorporates a differentiable parameterized graph constructor and an enhanced batch normalization technique. We evaluate our approach on the well-established Semantic3D benchmark and achieve state-of-the-art performance on various classification and semantic segmentation tasks across multiple datasets. Specifically, our method yields a 2-4% improvement in mean intersection over union (mIoU) compared to the current best approaches, with comparable computational complexity. Notably, GCN-Swish exhibits superior performance on datasets with highly occluded and fragmented point cloud configurations. The source code of this project is available at https://github.com/PC-semantic-gcn/semantic-gcn. Experimental evidence confirms the efficacy of our approach and its potential for application in other 3D computer vision tasks. With further adaptation, GCN-Swish has the potential to excel in other domains such as 3D object recognition and robotic mapping. Additionally, our research sheds light on the importance of spatial reasoning in 3D computer vision and the relative simplicity of semantic segmentation tasks. We hypothesize that these findings may also apply to other 3D vision tasks and consider GCN-Swish a versatile model with a broad range of potential applications beyond semantic segmentation. We have undertaken a thorough analysis of the elemental abundance patterns in stars that host terrestrial planets with sizes similar to those of Earth. Our goal is to gain a deeper understanding of the geological history and interior environments of these exoplanets. We utilized data from spectrographs with high resolution and covering a wide wavelength range to determine the elemental abundances of 19 elements in 12 stars that host terrestrial planets. These abundance patterns are then compared to those of solar analogs. We developed relationships between the elemental abundances of these stars and the masses of the planets they host, discovering correlations between the abundance of volatile elements and planetary mass. This relationship suggests more massive terrestrial planets tend to have higher volatile content. We also found the elemental abundance patterns of these stars vary based on the star's metallicity, with solar-like abundance patterns observed at solar metallicity. Our study provides a framework for understanding the geological history and interior environments of terrestrial exoplanets based on the detailed elemental abundance patterns of their host stars. Our analysis indicates that low-mass, volatile-rich exoplanets are more common around low-metallicity stars, while high-mass, non-volatile exoplanets are more common around high-metallicity stars. Our work also offers a potential explanation for the observed skewness of low-mass exoplanets towards being smaller than those with higher masses. Finally, our study indicates that solar elemental abundance is typical, and that the solar composition is likely the result of a late and moderate accretion of refractory and volatile materials. Our research provides a new perspective on planetary interior formation based on the detailed elemental abundance patterns of their host stars. This study investigates the conditions under which local data scrutiny, a concept
introduced in 2018 to address out-of-distribution issues in deep learning, can help
address a different challenge: improving model robustness against adversarial attacks.

model robustness and treat this problem as a robustness learning issue. Through
theoretical analysis and experiments, we identify the key factors that allow local data
scrutiny to enhance robustness, revealing a complex interplay with parameters and
data characteristics. The findings provide insights into the conditions necessary for
local data scrutiny to contribute to robust learning. The code for this research is
available at https://github.com/epf-lausanne/local-inquiry.

This approach treats variability as a temporal series and applies a probabilistic method to extract underlying patterns. Our results indicate that the autoencoder is capable of training on small datasets, and the inferred intrinsic temporal series aligns more closely with neighboring SN Ia amplitude and redshift. Additionally, the autoencoder's capabilities were further demonstrated by using it to generate "negative evolution" for a SN Ia that showed a decline phase, and the resulting intrinsic temporal series for this SN Ia matches those of SN Ia events with a standard lightcurve shape. Our method was developed using the PyTFA platform and tested with the SN Ia sample from the Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIS) program. This program aims to improve on existing methods that rely on near-infrared spectral observations, and our approach paves the way for further integration with photometric and other spectroscopic data to refine the precision of SN Ia cosmology. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, to capture more accurate dynamics, we model these events on hypergraphs, allowing individuals to interact with multiple groups at once. To find the threshold below which an epidemic will inevitably spread and that above which it will inevitably subside, we analyze a stochastic model on these hypergraphs. By assuming that transmission rates vary widely while average degrees remain relatively constant, we derive a precise extinction threshold. This threshold is expressed as the smallest eigenvalue of a certain matrix associated with the hypergraph. Additionally, we calculate the spectral limits for this matrix, providing a more detailed analysis near its smallest eigenvalue and initiating a broader investigation of these limits and their applications. Our methods also yield techniques for estimating the rapidity and likelihood of an epidemic's spread, giving rise to a new area of research within network epidemiology. As a testament to the validity of our approach, our simulations accurately predict the outcomes of complex disease transmissions on hypergraphs. These predictions are in line with existing research within the field. By applying our techniques to real-world scenarios, such as the spread of COVID-19 at a cruise ship, we demonstrate the potential for more refined modeling, leading to more precise and accurate forecasts. Ultimately, our work paves the way for improved and evidence-driven decision-making in the event of future epidemics.
